key_points: Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the biggest IPO ever, at about a $1.5 trillion valuation.
Notable's Series E bet at $61.5 billion implies a roughly 15x paper return.
GIC invested over $4.5 billion and Baillie Gifford $1.5 billion across three rounds each.

e2be825e0d55.headline: Trump's Third Meme Coin Gala Draws Fewer Whales and Louder Conflict-of-Interest Cries
body: Donald Trump is scheduled to headline his third crypto gala on Sunday night at the Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, a dinner that rewards the biggest holders of his own $TRUMP meme coin, according to The Guardian. Democrats are accusing the president of improperly profiting from his crypto ventures while in office.

The event website lists meet-and-greets with supporters including Floyd Mayweather, Kevin O'Leary, Tristan Thompson and mentalist Lior Suchard. Perks are tiered across 185 holders: 120 attendees get items such as a fragrance, a poster, a commemorative ticket and a Trump watch, the top 29 are invited to a VIP reception, and the top four win a gold watch.

The guest list is not what it used to be. Combined holdings among contestants fell from $148m in May 2025 to $8.6m for this month's gala. An analysis of blockchain data by the nonprofit Public Citizen, prepared for Reuters, found more than half of the wallets on the leaderboard are tied to exchanges that bar US users, suggesting foreign holders.

Money is the backdrop. Financial disclosures released in June show Trump made more than $1bn from crypto businesses since returning to office, including over $500m from World Liberty Financial and about $600m from meme coin sales. The meme coin alone has earned the family at least $635m, and the Trumps had earned at least $2.3bn through April from four main crypto ventures.

Outside investors have fared worse. A Reuters analysis found those in the family's five main crypto and crypto-linked projects have lost more than $5bn, with several assets at record lows. Trump's stake in Trump Media & Technology Group is worth about $430m.

Politically, Democrats say that after sweeping midterm wins they will investigate conflicts of interest and push legislation to ban events like this dinner. Senator Adam Schiff and eight colleagues wrote last month that the contest appears built to boost $TRUMP investment. The White House has said neither the president nor his family has ever engaged in conflicts of interest.
e2be825e0d55.summary: Trump headlines his third $TRUMP meme coin gala in Virginia as Democrats allege self-enrichment. Contestant holdings have collapsed to $8.6m from $148m, and many wallets appear foreign-linked.
e2be825e0d55.pixel_take: The VIP prize is a gold watch, which is fitting: holders have spent months watching their investment's value tick down.
e2be825e0d55.why_it_matters: The gala shows how political power and crypto can blur, a theme likely to shape regulation and congressional probes. Retail investors in celebrity-linked tokens face steep losses, as the $5bn drop for outside investors shows.
key_points: Gala at Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia rewards top $TRUMP holders
Contestant holdings fell from $148m to $8.6m; over half of wallets appear foreign-linked
Democrats plan probes and legislation; outside investors in Trump crypto projects lost over $5bn

909c7891b599.headline: Second ship hit in naval drone attacks off Libya's Benghazi coast
body: A commercial vessel flying a Maltese flag has become the second ship targeted in a string of naval drone attacks off Benghazi, in eastern Libya, according to Al Jazeera.

Libyan forces reportedly intercepted more than 20 naval drones during the incident. The report does not say who launched them, what damage was done, or whether anyone was hurt, so those questions remain open.

The attack followed an earlier drone strike the same day on a Russian ship docked at a naval base in Benghazi. Two vessels linked to different flags being targeted within hours suggests a coordinated pattern, though the source material does not confirm that or point to any perpetrator.

The episode matters because Benghazi sits on the Mediterranean coast, a busy corridor for trade and energy shipments. Naval drones are cheap and hard to spot, and have changed maritime conflict elsewhere by letting small actors threaten expensive ships.

Attacks on commercial shipping tend to ripple outward. Insurers raise war-risk premiums, shipowners reconsider routes, and energy traders watch for any hint of disruption. Libya is an oil producer, so instability near its ports always draws market attention.
Details are still thin. Until authorities or an identified party explain who was behind the attacks and what was hit, the full scale of the incident is unclear.
909c7891b599.summary: A Maltese-flagged commercial ship was targeted off Benghazi after a drone attack on a Russian ship at a naval base. Libyan forces reportedly intercepted more than 20 naval drones.
909c7891b599.why_it_matters: Attacks on ships in the Mediterranean can raise insurance costs and rattle energy and shipping markets. Libya is an oil producer, so port security there is closely watched by traders. Cheap naval drones make such threats harder to defend against.
key_points: A Maltese-flagged commercial vessel was targeted off Benghazi, the second ship attacked.
Libyan forces reportedly intercepted more than 20 naval drones.
Earlier that day, a drone attack hit a Russian ship docked at a Benghazi naval base.

19f8e32a1da2.headline: Copper Bounces Back After a 9% Tumble Tied to AI Demand Worries
body: Copper prices rose after a sharp 9% drop last week, according to Investing.com, which linked the slide to concerns about demand from artificial intelligence. The report is brief, and the details behind the rebound were not available.

The headline points to AI as the source of the worry. Copper is a core industrial metal used in power grids, wiring, and electronics, and AI data centers have become a big part of the story investors tell about future demand. When that story wobbles, a metal tied to it can swing hard.

A 9% weekly fall is large for a commodity that is usually seen as a slow-moving barometer of industrial activity. A bounce afterward is common in markets, where sharp declines often attract bargain hunters. But a single up day does not show whether the drop was an overreaction or the start of a longer reset.

The material does not give price levels, the size of the rebound, or what specifically sparked the AI concerns, so we will not guess. What it does show is how closely copper traders are now watching the technology sector for clues about demand.
For now, the takeaway is simple: the market got spooked, then took a breath. Whether the AI demand questions get answered or grow louder is what will decide where copper heads next.
19f8e32a1da2.summary: Copper prices rose after a 9% drop last week that Investing.com tied to concerns over AI demand. Details on the size of the rebound were not available.
19f8e32a1da2.pixel_take: Copper fell 9% on AI worries, then bounced. Even industrial metals are now checking the tech headlines before getting out of bed.
19f8e32a1da2.why_it_matters: Copper is a bellwether for industrial and infrastructure demand, so big swings can signal shifting expectations about growth. If AI-driven demand is doubted, miners, manufacturers, and investors in commodities may need to reprice their outlooks.
key_points: Copper rose after a 9% drop last week.
Investing.com linked the drop to AI demand concerns.
Details on the size of the rebound were not provided.

ac9b29d220cb.headline: S&P 500 Futures Edge Up, Offering Wall Street a Breather After a Rough Week
body: Stock futures tied to the S&P 500 rose in early trading on Sunday evening, according to The New York Times, suggesting investors may get a calmer start when regular trading resumes on Monday after a difficult week for markets.

Futures are contracts that let investors bet on where an index will open before the opening bell. They trade almost around the clock, so they work as a rough early weather report for the stock market. A rise points to a steadier open, but it guarantees nothing.
The Times reported that analysts cautioned more volatility could still be ahead. That is the polite market way of saying the sun may be out, but you should keep the umbrella nearby.

The material provided gives no detail on what drove last week's losses or how large the futures gain was, so it is hard to say how much of the optimism is conviction and how much is simply relief after a bruising stretch. Early moves in futures often fade or reverse once real money starts flowing on Monday morning.

For everyday investors, the lesson is familiar. One quiet night in futures does not make a trend, and a tough week is not a reason to rewrite a long-term plan. Still, the S&P 500 sits inside many retirement accounts and index funds, so even small swings get noticed by a lot of people.
ac9b29d220cb.summary: S&P 500 futures rose in early trading, hinting at a steadier Monday open after a tough week, though analysts warned more volatility could still be ahead, according to The New York Times.
ac9b29d220cb.pixel_take: Futures are up, which is Wall Street's way of exhaling. Analysts say don't get comfortable, so everyone is holding their breath again right after.
ac9b29d220cb.why_it_matters: The S&P 500 underpins many retirement accounts and index funds, so shifts in sentiment can touch ordinary portfolios. Early futures moves are a hint, not a promise, and warnings of volatility suggest caution is still warranted.
key_points: S&P 500 futures rose in early trading ahead of Monday's open.
The move follows a tough week for investors.
Analysts warned more volatility could still lie ahead.

3bb0094b63d9.headline: Physicists Send a Text Message Using Gravity, and Yes, an Elevator Counterweight Was the Pen
body: Physicists at the University of Queensland have sent what New Atlas describes as the first message transmitted by gravity. By moving an elevator's roughly 4,000-pound (1,815 kg) counterweight in a timed pattern, they encoded ones and zeros and spelled out a single word: "Gravity." The study was published in Science Advances in 2026.

The setup was simple. The two positions of the counterweight stood for zero and one. On the other side of a wall, a commercial gravimeter, which uses a spring-mounted mass, picked up tiny shifts in the vertical pull of gravity. Moving the counterweight changed the measured acceleration by about 50 nanometers per second squared, roughly five billionths of Earth's ordinary pull.

It was not fast. Each bit got a full minute: 25 seconds to move the weight, 10 to settle and 25 to average the readings. After correcting for Earth's tides and instrument drift, the team recovered all 49 bits, plus the start and end markers. The whole transmission took 63 minutes.

The appeal is that gravity has no known equivalent of a Faraday cage. A metal mesh can disrupt radio waves, but no material is known to screen out a gravitational pull. The researchers say a better gravimeter and a faster elevator could reach about 15 bits per minute. Under optimistic assumptions, including a 75-metric-ton mass and a noisier signal, the range could stretch to roughly 1,640 feet (500 meters).

The idea grew out of an attempt to weigh trucks without having them drive onto a scale. For comparison, a 2012 Fermilab experiment sent a neutrino signal through about 790 feet of earth at six bits per minute, but it needed a particle accelerator. This one needed an elevator and an off-the-shelf sensor.

Big caveats remain. Vibrations or other moving masses could drown out the message, so a lot more work is needed before this is practical. Still, the authors note that drowning out a signal is different from blocking it with a wall.
3bb0094b63d9.summary: Queensland physicists moved an elevator counterweight to send the word "Gravity" through a wall as binary code, detected by a gravimeter. It took 63 minutes, but gravity can't be shielded like radio.
3bb0094b63d9.pixel_take: An hour for one word is slower than your aunt's group chat, but at least this message can't be blocked by a wall, a tunnel or a bad Wi-Fi router.
3bb0094b63d9.why_it_matters: Wireless communication depends on signals that walls, water and metal can block. A channel that cannot be shielded, even at a snail's pace, could one day matter for niche uses where nothing else gets through. For now it is a proof of concept, but it shows how cheaper, more sensitive sensors keep opening new technology frontiers.
key_points: Researchers sent 49 bits spelling "Gravity" by moving an elevator counterweight, in 63 minutes.
A commercial gravimeter detected a shift of about 50 nanometers per second squared through a wall.
Better gear might reach 15 bits per minute and about 500 meters, but vibrations remain a problem.

1be9a8552240.headline: GOP Lawmaker Is 'Optimistic' Congress Can Pass an AI Bill Before the Clock Runs Out
body: Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) said on Sunday that he is "optimistic" Congress can pass a bipartisan artificial intelligence bill before the end of the year, according to The Hill.

The timing is tight. The teaser notes that the window is narrowing for Republicans to advance legislation before Democrats take control, which means the lame-duck stretch is the last easy chance for the current majority to get its priorities across the line.

The material available does not spell out what the bill would contain, how it would be paired with other legislation, or who has signed on from either party. So for now, the one solid fact is the word "bipartisan" and the confidence of one lawmaker who works on the issue.

Context helps here. Washington has spent years talking about how to regulate AI, from safety rules to questions about who sets the standards, and comprehensive federal law has been hard to pass. End-of-year sessions are often crowded, and big bills tend to get squeezed by deadlines and competing priorities.

Optimism from a sponsor is not a vote count, and it is worth watching whether leaders in both chambers make floor time for the measure. If it stalls, any AI legislation would have to start over in a new Congress with a different balance of power.
1be9a8552240.summary: Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) says he is optimistic a bipartisan AI bill can pass before year-end, even as the window closes for Republicans to act before Democrats take control.
1be9a8552240.pixel_take: Passing an AI bill in a lame-duck session is a bit like training for a marathon the week of the race: optimism is free, but the clock is not.
1be9a8552240.why_it_matters: Federal AI rules would shape how tech companies build and deploy products, and the cost of compliance could affect valuations and investment. Clear rules can also reduce uncertainty for businesses, while a stalled bill leaves a patchwork and more delay.
key_points: Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) said Sunday he is optimistic about passing a bipartisan AI bill this year.
The window is narrowing before Democrats take control.
Details of the bill were not provided in the available material.

e7090200216e.headline: Microsoft and US officials warn: the big tech outages are not done yet
body: Over roughly the past week, the US has seen a nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Outlook outage that left whole companies idle, and a banking outage at JPMorgan Chase, according to The Verge. Now Microsoft and the US government are both saying the string of breakdowns may not be over.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN that Americans should expect heavy investment in upgrading systems and in cybersecurity. He added that any big leap in computing power and applications tends to come with "bumps in the road."

Microsoft President Brad Smith struck a darker note on CBS's Face the Nation. He said people should be prepared for the coming months, because this kind of work doesn't get done in a couple of weeks, and described the world's information infrastructure as being upgraded right now.

The outages of the past week were believed to be caused by cyberattacks, according to the report. Smith argued that AI makes it easier to find flaws in software. Defenders can use that knowledge to patch code, while bad actors can use it to break into systems.
The pressure is not limited to the past week. The Verge notes a recent rise in attacks on government and commercial systems, including at the USDA, JPMorgan and supermarkets.

Whether the next failure comes from AI-assisted hackers or from human error during a rushed patching effort on aging systems, the message from both Microsoft and Washington is the same: more is likely coming.
e7090200216e.summary: Microsoft's Brad Smith and DNI Jay Clayton say more major outages are likely after a week of FAA, Outlook and JPMorgan disruptions, as AI speeds up both the finding and the fixing of software flaws.
e7090200216e.pixel_take: When the people running the systems and the people guarding the country both say 'brace yourselves,' maybe keep a paper calendar and a spare phone charger handy.
e7090200216e.why_it_matters: Outages at an airline regulator, an email giant and a major bank show how much daily commerce rides on a few systems. Expect rising spending on cybersecurity and system upgrades, and possible disruption to payments, travel and work in the meantime.
key_points: A nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Outlook outage and a JPMorgan Chase banking outage hit within about a week.
Microsoft's Brad Smith and DNI Jay Clayton both warned more outages are likely in the coming months.
Smith said AI makes finding software flaws easier, which helps both patchers and hackers.

a4537224b7d2.headline: Bitcoin bounces off cycle low near $55,111, while Ledger probes tampered devices in Berlin and the UAE
body: Bitcoin has rebounded sharply from what Cointelegraph's weekly Hodler's Digest calls a new cycle low, with $55,111 cited as the level in question. The big open question for traders: was that the bottom, or just a trampoline before another dip?

The teaser does not say how large the bounce was or what drove it, so we will not guess. What it does make clear is that the market is now debating whether the lows are in. Sharp rebounds after a steep drop are common in crypto, and they often tempt traders to call a bottom early.

In a separate storyline, hardware wallet maker Ledger is investigating new reports of tampered devices in Berlin and the UAE, according to Cointelegraph. The headline says more tampered Ledgers were found, which suggests this is not the first such report, though the material provided gives no further details.

Tampering reports matter because hardware wallets exist to keep private keys away from the internet. If a device is altered before it reaches the owner, that promise is in question. The general advice in crypto circles is to buy directly from the manufacturer or authorized sellers and to check for signs of tampering on arrival.

Taken together, the two stories show the two kinds of risk crypto holders face: price swings in the market, and security risks in how they store their coins. Ledger has not been quoted in the material available, so the scale and cause of the problem remain to be confirmed.
a4537224b7d2.summary: Bitcoin rebounded sharply from a new cycle low of $55,111, leaving traders asking if the bottom is in. Meanwhile, Ledger is investigating fresh reports of tampered devices in Berlin and the UAE.
a4537224b7d2.pixel_take: Bitcoin bounced like it had a spring-loaded floor, and Ledger owners got a reminder: check the box before you trust the vault. Even the safe needs a safety check.
a4537224b7d2.why_it_matters: A possible price bottom shapes how investors size up risk, and a sharp rebound can be a trap as easily as a turning point. Tampered hardware wallets are a reminder that self-custody only protects your money if the device is trustworthy from day one.
key_points: Bitcoin rebounded sharply from a new cycle low, cited at $55,111.
Analysts and traders are debating whether that level is the true bottom.
Ledger is investigating new reports of tampered devices in Berlin and the UAE.

86845f971107.headline: Poland says Russia twice tried to kill Ukrainian-American rapper Kyivstoner, after Denmark's own plot claim
body: Poland has confirmed that Russian intelligence tried to assassinate Ukrainian-American rapper Albert Vasiliev, who performs as Kyivstoner, during a visit in August. A Polish Foreign Ministry spokesman, Maciej Wewior, confirmed the alleged plot to the Associated Press on Sunday, according to Al Jazeera.

The confirmation followed Denmark's announcement on Friday that Moscow had allegedly targeted the same man on Danish soil. Poland's Foreign Ministry called it the second attempt on the same person, saying the first was foiled in Poland in August 2026. Police detained a suspect, allegedly recruited by Moscow, on August 7.

In Denmark, the intelligence agency PET said it suspects Russia planned a killing at a concert in a Copenhagen suburb in September, with help from a banned Danish gang. Two Danish men appeared in court on Friday charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and attempted murder. Denmark also expelled a Russian diplomat. Russia's embassy in Copenhagen dismissed the allegations as unsubstantiated.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk had flagged the Warsaw plot on August 13 without naming the target, saying only that the person was uncomfortable for Putin's government. Vasiliev has voiced support for Ukraine and toured Europe this year before his concerts were cancelled for security reasons. Russia's FSB has accused him of involvement in supplying drones for an alleged attack on a defence enterprise near Moscow; DR reported that he denies this.

The diplomatic fallout may go beyond expulsions. Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said Denmark is considering suspending Schengen visas for Russians, and Poland said it backs measures to limit Russian nationals' travel in the EU. Western officials have accused Russia and its proxies of dozens of attacks and incidents across Europe since the 2022 full-scale invasion.
86845f971107.summary: Poland confirmed Russian intelligence allegedly tried to kill Ukrainian-American rapper Kyivstoner in August, after Denmark described a second plot. Copenhagen expelled a diplomat and weighs suspending Schengen visas for Russians.
86845f971107.why_it_matters: Alleged state-backed plots on European soil raise security costs and push governments toward tougher sanctions and travel limits. Restrictions such as suspended Schengen visas could further strain EU-Russia relations and add to geopolitical risk for markets.
key_points: Poland says it foiled a Russian-linked assassination attempt on rapper Kyivstoner in August; Denmark alleges a second plot in September.
Two Danish men are charged, and Denmark expelled a Russian diplomat; Russia calls the claims unsubstantiated.
Denmark is considering suspending Schengen visas for Russians, with Poland's backing.

6ee0a6470460.headline: Energy bills set to jump 26% in January: how to keep the damage down
body: Household energy bills in Great Britain are forecast to rise by 26% for millions of homes in January, according to BBC News. Experts say there are still practical ways to keep spending in check, even as the unit price of gas in particular is set to climb.

The key point is that Ofgem's price cap, like suppliers' fixed deals, limits the price of each unit of energy, not your total bill. You pay for what you use, so consumption is the one lever you control. After years of relatively high prices, many people have already cut back, but experts suggest taking a fresh look and renewing good habits.

The tips are small but add up. Turn down the flow temperature on a combi boiler, switch off the pre-heat function that keeps water warm when unused, and consider lowering the thermostat by one degree, though 18C is the recommended minimum. Washing clothes at 30C, blocking draughts and batch cooking also help. Thick clothes, blankets and hot drinks are the low-tech option.

How you pay matters too. Ofgem says about five million people still pay when a bill arrives every three months. Regular meter readings or a smart meter, plus a monthly direct debit, avoid estimated bills. Paying by direct debit is typically £138 a year cheaper than standard credit. Prepayment customers now pay slightly less than the capped direct debit variable rate.

Fixed tariffs lock the unit price but not the total bill. Judging them is tricky right now: some fixes sit below the next cap level, but if prices fall sharply, a long fix could look poor value. Which? urges close attention to exit fees, and MoneySavingExpert advises comparing every deal on the market, not just your own supplier's.

Help is available. The government will pay £100 to millions of homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with equivalents expected in Scotland and Wales. Anyone on means-tested benefits gets £150 off electricity this winter, and many pensioners get the winter fuel payment. Hardship grants, the Fuel Direct Scheme and insulation grants exist too, but beware of scams posing as official schemes.
6ee0a6470460.summary: Energy bills are forecast to rise 26% in January. Experts urge cutting usage, paying by direct debit and comparing fixed deals carefully, while government support of £100 to £150 is available for many households.
6ee0a6470460.pixel_take: The price cap caps the price per unit, not your ability to wince at the bill. Time to bring back the blanket, the hot drink and the noble art of draught-blocking.
6ee0a6470460.why_it_matters: A 26% jump in energy costs squeezes household budgets and can feed into inflation and spending elsewhere. Knowing how caps, fixed deals and payment methods work can save real money, with some households saving £138 a year just by paying differently.
key_points: Energy prices are forecast to rise 26% for millions of homes in January.
Direct debit is typically £138 a year cheaper than standard credit.
Support includes £100 for bands A to D in England and £150 off electricity for those on means-tested benefits.

6d6290d67ed7.headline: An ad-tech stock is up 52% in November, and investors are asking if the party has legs
body: A headline from Investing.com, published on November 23, 2026, asks whether a 52% November surge in an ad-tech stock marks the beginning or the end of its run. The stock is described as being picked by an AI model.

That is essentially all the material tells us. The teaser is empty and the full article was not available, so the company's name, the drivers behind the rally and any analyst views are unknown to us. We are not going to guess at them.

What we can say is that a 52% gain in a single month is a big move for any stock. Moves like that usually come with higher volatility, and they often attract momentum traders as well as long-term investors. Both groups can reverse course quickly.

The mention of an AI-picked label also reflects a wider trend: stock-screening tools and AI models are increasingly used to surface candidates, and retail investors pay attention. Still, a model's pick is a starting point, not a guarantee, and a sharp run-up can mean much of the good news is already in the price.

The start-or-end question in the headline is the classic one after a rally. Without details on earnings, valuation or the catalyst, nobody can answer it responsibly, and readers should check the original Investing.com piece and company filings before acting.
6d6290d67ed7.summary: Investing.com asks whether a 52% November rally in an AI-picked ad-tech stock is the beginning or the end of its run. Few details were available, so the story is mostly a caution on chasing big monthly gains.
6d6290d67ed7.pixel_take: A 52% month is the stock market's version of a sugar rush: thrilling, and everyone's asking what happens at the crash. Even the robots picking winners can't promise the next chapter.
6d6290d67ed7.why_it_matters: Huge one-month rallies can lure investors in near the top, and the risk of sharp reversals rises with them. AI-generated stock picks are becoming more visible, but they don't replace checking fundamentals and valuation before putting your own money to work.
key_points: An ad-tech stock is reported up 52% in November, per Investing.com.
The stock is described as AI-picked; the company name and catalysts weren't available.
Rallies of this size raise the question of whether momentum can last or reverses.

6e76b6ad97e6.headline: Windows Spring Cleaning: 8 Apps Engadget Says Deserve the Boot
body: Engadget has published a list of eight Windows apps it says you should consider removing or replacing, ranging from pre-installed bloatware to popular third-party tools that have better, often free, alternatives. The piece, dated November 23, 2026, argues that bloatware and adware feel more common than ever.

The cost is real, according to the article: these apps eat SSD space, which is pricier now because of soaring storage prices, and they can use up RAM and pepper you with alerts. That is why debloating a fresh Windows PC has become routine.

On media and video, Engadget suggests swapping the built-in Media Player for VLC, which plays many formats without extra codecs. It also pitches CapCut over Microsoft's Clipchamp, whose flashier features, like 4K export and Copilot integration, sit behind a Microsoft 365 paywall. CapCut has a subscription too, starting at $19.99 per month, but the author calls it good value.

Then come the usual suspects. uTorrent is flagged for ads, bundled extras and a 2015 scandal in which it installed a Litecoin miner; qBittorrent and Transmission are named as replacements. Trial versions of Norton or McAfee are labeled unneeded for most people, since Windows Defender is deemed enough for basic protection. The built-in News and Weather apps are dismissed as ad-heavy and low-quality.

The Xbox app is worth keeping only if you game on PC, the article says, and Steam-only players or ex-Game Pass subscribers can skip it. Microsoft Solitaire Collection, which charges $1.49 per month for the premium edition, can be replaced by free browser games or a Steam version with no ads.

Finally, the free Microsoft Office trials that ship with Windows are described as subscription nudges. Google Docs or OnlyOffice can cover most needs, though Engadget notes many professionals still need Office because .docx and .xlsx are corporate standards. Microsoft 365 costs at least $9.99 per month or $99.99 per year.
6e76b6ad97e6.summary: Engadget lists eight Windows apps worth removing or replacing, from bloatware and antivirus trials to ad-laden games, citing free alternatives and the cost of wasted storage and memory.
6e76b6ad97e6.pixel_take: Your new PC arrives with more trial offers than a gym lobby. Deleting them is the cheapest upgrade you'll make this year, and unlike the subscriptions, it doesn't bill monthly.
6e76b6ad97e6.why_it_matters: With storage prices rising, reclaiming SSD space and RAM from bloatware has real value. Swapping paid or trial software for free alternatives can also trim recurring subscription costs on a household budget.
key_points: Engadget names eight Windows apps to remove or replace, including uTorrent, Norton/McAfee trials and Office trials.
Free alternatives like VLC, qBittorrent, OnlyOffice and Windows Defender can cover most needs.
Bloatware eats SSD space and RAM, which matters more as storage prices climb.

6738e42a373d.headline: Mayor Mamdani Releases 84,000 More 9/11 Records After Earlier Batch Showed Air Quality Claims Were False
body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democrat, has released another 84,000 records tied to the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks, according to The Hill. The new batch follows an earlier release that, per the report, showed city leaders lied about air quality after the attacks.

The material available is thin: the teaser quotes the start of a Mamdani statement about the attacks but does not say what the new records contain. So far, the clear facts are the volume of documents and the context of the earlier disclosure.

That context matters. In the days after the World Trade Center collapsed, New Yorkers were told about the safety of the air around Lower Manhattan. The earlier release, as described by The Hill, indicated those assurances were not truthful. Many residents, workers and responders were exposed to dust and debris during that period.

Publishing a pile of records this size is the kind of move that tends to keep reporters, lawyers and public health advocates busy for a long time. Eighty-four thousand documents is not a light weekend read, and what they show will depend on what researchers find once they dig in.

For now, the release signals that Mamdani's administration is willing to open the city's files on one of the most sensitive chapters in its modern history. Further details on the contents are likely to emerge as the records are reviewed.
6738e42a373d.summary: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani released 84,000 more records on the 9/11 attacks, following an earlier release that reportedly showed city leaders lied about air quality, according to The Hill.
6738e42a373d.why_it_matters: Government transparency about post-9/11 conditions bears on public trust, health-related claims and potential legal or compensation questions. Large document releases can shape how cities are held accountable for public safety statements in a crisis.
key_points: Mayor Zohran Mamdani released 84,000 more 9/11-related records.
An earlier release reportedly showed city leaders lied about air quality.
The contents of the new batch have not yet been detailed.

7e276867e62f.headline: Molly Meldrum, the Stetson-wearing Guru of Australian pop on Countdown, dies at 83
body: Molly Meldrum, the Australian music journalist, broadcaster and producer who hosted the ABC's Countdown, died peacefully in the early hours of Monday at a Melbourne hospital. He was 83. His longtime friend and manager, Mark Klemens, confirmed the news to The Guardian.

Klemens called him "a true Australian icon" who opened doors for many. Meldrum's partner, Yan Wongngam, and his family said in a statement that he was affectionately dubbed "the Guru" and was the heartbeat and champion of Australian music. They thanked staff at Epworth Richmond for their care.

On Countdown, which ran on Sunday evenings from 1974 to 1987, Meldrum is credited with helping break Abba, Blondie and Madonna in Australia. Songs such as Madonna's Holiday and Duran Duran's Planet Earth went from unknowns to Top 10 hits after his backing. He also gave early exposure to local acts including INXS, Kylie Minogue, Skyhooks and Mental as Anything.

His on-air style was famously shambolic. He held LPs up awkwardly under harsh studio lights, and because ABC rules barred hosts from endorsing products, his catchphrase became "do yourself a favour". Prime Minister Anthony Albanese paid tribute on X, praising his enthusiasm and his support for Australian artists. Elton John once called him the single most important influence in Australian pop music.

Born Ian Meldrum in Orbost, Victoria, he was one of the first openly gay personalities on Australian television. He survived a serious fall from a ladder in 2011 that required surgery for head and spinal injuries. He was made a member of the Order of Australia in 1986 and became the first non-recording artist inducted into the Aria Hall of Fame in 2014. He is survived by his partner, adopted son and two younger brothers.
7e276867e62f.summary: Molly Meldrum, the Countdown host who helped launch global and Australian acts alike, has died aged 83 in a Melbourne hospital, his manager confirmed. Tributes have come from the prime minister and the music world.
7e276867e62f.why_it_matters: Meldrum's career shows how much a single trusted tastemaker could shape record sales and careers before streaming algorithms took over. His influence helped build Australia's music industry and its international reach.
key_points: Molly Meldrum died aged 83 at a Melbourne hospital, confirmed by his manager Mark Klemens.
He hosted ABC's Countdown from 1974 to 1987, boosting Abba, Blondie, Madonna and Australian acts like INXS and Kylie Minogue.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Elton John were among those praising his influence.

c56921972084.headline: Your Smart Glasses Can Moonlight as a Teleprompter, and Engadget Says They're Good at It
body: Smart glasses with built-in waveguide displays, including the XGIMI MemoMind One and Even Realities G2, come with a teleprompter mode that lets you read a script while keeping eye contact with your audience, according to a hands-on guide from Engadget's Harish Jonnalagadda.

Setup is simple. You load a script into the companion app and choose how quickly the text scrolls. The G2 accepts PDF, plaintext and DOCX files, while the MemoMind One handles only TXT and DOCX. Converting a PDF is easy, but it is still an extra chore.

Both models offer an auto-follow feature that speeds up or slows down the text to match how fast you talk. Engadget notes that it supposedly relies on AI to do this. You can also set auto-scroll by words per minute or scroll manually. The MemoMind One gives you more control over the display, including font size, line width and teleprompter-only display scaling.

In testing, the reviewer read a video review script off the MicroLED-based monochrome waveguides and said the text did not block his view. A timer, battery level and clock are also shown. The text is hard for onlookers to see unless they stand within about 15cm, and it was readable outdoors, with the MemoMind One getting brighter than the G2. Since the glasses move with you, you aren't stuck behind a lectern or a dedicated prompter.

Beyond the teleprompter, Engadget prefers the MemoMind One. It has built-in Harman-tuned audio, better battery life, a physical button rather than the G2's temple-tip gestures, and three frame styles against two. Both weigh under 50g, and the G2 is lighter. Neither has a camera.
On price, the MemoMind One costs $499, $100 less than the G2. Prescription lenses add $280 for the MemoMind One and $159 for the G2. The reviewer says he would pick the MemoMind One.
c56921972084.summary: Engadget says waveguide smart glasses like the MemoMind One and Even G2 work well as teleprompters, with auto-follow scrolling and outdoor readability. The reviewer prefers the cheaper $499 MemoMind One.
c56921972084.pixel_take: A teleprompter that follows you around and nobody else can read. Finally, a gadget that helps you fake confidence and keeps the secret.
c56921972084.why_it_matters: Smart glasses are searching for everyday uses beyond novelty, and a practical task like speechmaking is an easy one to understand. Spending $499 or more makes sense only if a device does several jobs well, so features like this help justify the price.
key_points: MemoMind One and Even G2 have teleprompter modes with auto-follow, auto-scroll and manual control.
The MemoMind One offers finer display controls but doesn't read PDFs; the G2 does.
The MemoMind One costs $499, $100 less than the G2, and Engadget's reviewer prefers it.

46084e3539a8.headline: Clariant and CD&R reportedly circle Ashland in takeover talks
body: Swiss specialty chemicals group Clariant and private equity firm CD&R are in talks to acquire Ashland, according to a Bloomberg report relayed by Investing.com on November 23, 2026.

That is essentially the whole public record for now. The headline does not say how much is on the table, how the two suitors would split the spoils, or how far along the talks are. Nothing has been confirmed in the material we have, so treat this as a report of talks, not a done deal.

The pairing is notable all the same. A strategic buyer like Clariant typically brings industry know-how and possible cost savings, while a private equity firm like CD&R brings financing muscle and a taste for restructuring. Teaming up can let both share the price tag and the risk, though it also means two sets of priorities at one table.

Talks like these often fizzle. Price, financing, regulatory hurdles and shareholder appetite can all derail a deal, and companies in these situations usually say little until something is signed. Readers should wait for official statements from the companies involved.

For investors, the takeaway is simple: a reported approach tends to put a company on the radar of deal watchers, but a report is not an offer, and an offer is not a closing. Until the parties speak, the details remain unknown.
46084e3539a8.summary: Clariant and CD&R are reportedly in talks to acquire Ashland, according to Bloomberg via Investing.com. No price, structure or timeline was included in the material, and nothing is confirmed.
46084e3539a8.pixel_take: Two suitors, one target, zero published details. In dealmaking, this is the awkward group-chat stage before anyone agrees on who's paying for dinner.
46084e3539a8.why_it_matters: Reported takeover talks can move the shares of companies involved and signal consolidation in specialty chemicals. But without confirmed terms, they are a rumor-grade signal, so investors should be cautious about reacting to the headline alone.
key_points: Bloomberg reports Clariant and CD&R are in talks to acquire Ashland.
No price, structure or timeline is given in the available material.
The talks are unconfirmed and may not lead to a deal.

05aab9fe7b4a.headline: Poundland's Tills Are Busy, But Its Owner Holds the Purse Strings and a Deadline Looms
body: Poundland, the discount chain with 600 stores across the UK and Ireland, has days to find a buyer or risk collapsing into administration, according to BBC News. The deadline was recently extended by 10 days, buying the business a short reprieve.

The odd part is that shoppers haven't gone anywhere. Over the year to September, Poundland swung from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges. First-quarter like-for-like sales rose 7%, and Halloween sales were 11.4% higher than last year. Insolvency specialist Julie Palmer of Begbies Traynor called it a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse.

The ownership bit is where it gets tangled. US investment firm Gordon Brothers bought Poundland from Pepco for £1 last year, put it up for sale in September, then rejected offers that would have kept it going. It is also one of the company's lenders, owed money including a £22.5m shareholder loan it inherited. It has frozen about £50m in funds, though it recently released around £21m over two weeks.

That matters because a lender-owner is first in line for repayment in a collapse, while suppliers are not. Gordon Brothers says Poundland remains vulnerable to any downturn, and argues a break-up could protect jobs because buyers of the stores would have to keep staff. Critics say it is running the business down to profit from insolvency, which the firm denies.

Two bids are known: Irish firm Martin Property Group wants to buy it as a going concern, while Xyra Group has also bid, though doubts remain about its credibility. About 11,000 jobs are at stake, plus those at suppliers.

Politics has joined the party. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds have demanded answers on why the Martin offer was rejected, and a committee of MPs questioned the firm last week. Retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth says Gordon Brothers appears unmoved. With Christmas looming, empty shelves in November and December could be the real killer.
05aab9fe7b4a.summary: Poundland has days to find a buyer or face administration despite improving sales and profits. Its US owner, also a main lender, has restricted cash and rejected offers, drawing political pressure.
05aab9fe7b4a.pixel_take: Poundland's customers are doing their bit, but when your owner is also your banker, the shelves may be the only thing getting cleared out.
05aab9fe7b4a.why_it_matters: Up to 11,000 jobs and many supplier businesses depend on the outcome, and it shows how financing and ownership structures can sink a retailer that is trading well. It also hints at wider risks for high street chains owned by lenders-turned-investors.
key_points: Poundland has 600 stores and 11,000 staff, and faces administration unless a buyer emerges after a 10-day extension.
Sales and profit improved, but owner and lender Gordon Brothers has restricted cash and rejected offers.
Martin Property Group and Xyra Group have bid, with political pressure on Gordon Brothers rising.

b1b92a46cd7e.headline: Congress Stuffs Itself With Turkey, Then Returns to a Year-End To-Do List the Size of a Parade Float
body: Lawmakers are heading home for the Thanksgiving break, according to The Hill, but the vacation will be short. When they return, they face a packed legislative agenda with only a few weeks left in the year.

The clock matters because of a major political shift. Per The Hill's report, Democrats are set to take control of both chambers in January, which leaves Republicans a narrow window to push through their priorities while they still hold the gavels.

The source material is a short preview, and the full details of the agenda were not available to us. We are therefore not going to guess which bills are on the list or how likely they are to pass. What the teaser makes clear is the structure of the moment: a deadline, a break, and a lot of work squeezed in between.

Some context helps. A final stretch before a change in power is often called a lame-duck session. The party on its way out can try to move legislation that would get harder, or impossible, once it loses control. Year-end periods also tend to attract must-do items, since Congress often saves its hardest decisions for the last possible moment.

For everyone outside Washington, the practical takeaway is simple: what gets done, or left undone, in these weeks can shape the starting conditions for the new Congress. Markets, businesses and households tend to watch such sessions for signs of policy certainty or fresh gridlock.
b1b92a46cd7e.summary: Lawmakers are on Thanksgiving break but return to a crowded year-end agenda. With Democrats set to control both chambers in January, Republicans have only a few weeks to act, The Hill reports.
b1b92a46cd7e.pixel_take: Congress gets a few days of leftovers, then returns to the oldest tradition on Capitol Hill: doing everything at the last minute, now with a hard deadline and a changing of the guard.
b1b92a46cd7e.why_it_matters: A change in congressional control can reshape tax, spending and regulatory policy, so the final weeks of one-party control can set the stage for what comes next. 3ecf1ecb43f0.headline: Iran Says Tankers Set Ablaze in Strait of Hormuz as IRGC Warns of Enemy-Backed Unrest
body: Iran's navy claims that tankers breaking its rules were set on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Al Jazeera's live coverage of the Iran war. The report was published on November 22, 2026. The headline and teaser give no further detail on the vessels, their owners or the extent of any damage.

In a separate statement, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said that unnamed 'enemies' were trying to stoke unrest. The material does not say where the alleged unrest would occur or what evidence supports the claim, so the assertion should be treated as Iran's own account.

The material does not specify which rules the tankers allegedly violated, nor has any independent confirmation of the incident been provided in the text available to us. Claims made by a party to a conflict about its own military actions are best read with caution until verified by shipping data, insurers or other governments.

Some general context helps explain why this matters. The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway through which a large share of the world's seaborne oil passes, so any attack or harassment of tankers there tends to be watched closely by energy traders and shipping firms. Even the threat of disruption can raise insurance costs and rattle oil prices.

For now, the picture is incomplete: a claim of burning tankers and a warning about unrest, both from Iranian sources as relayed by Al Jazeera. Further reporting should clarify whether commercial shipping has actually been hit and how other countries respond.

152623e56e8c.headline: PlainApp links your Android phone to your PC wirelessly, free, with nothing to install on the computer
body: Engadget has highlighted PlainApp, a free, open-source Android app that lets you view and manage your phone's files from a Windows PC over Wi-Fi. It needs no account, no subscription and no extra software on the computer, according to the outlet's review.

Setup is short. PlainApp is on the Play Store and supports Android 9 or newer. You install it, grant notification and file access permissions, and note the URL it shows. With the PC on the same Wi-Fi network, you open that URL in any web browser.

There is one speed bump. PlainApp uses a self-signed TLS certificate, so the browser throws up a warning on first visit. You click Advanced, then Proceed, then Log in, and tap Allow on the phone when asked.

Once connected, you can see images, videos, music and contacts from your browser. The Files tab handles browsing and two-way transfers. You can also send text to the phone's clipboard, place a call from the web interface, and mirror the phone's screen in the browser.

Engadget's reviewer noted that PlainApp claims remote control is possible, similar to iPhone Mirroring on macOS, but could not get it to work on their phone. The media viewer shows images and videos in original quality, and converts HEVC video to H.264 if the browser cannot play it. There is also a basic image editor and a music player.
The verdict: Quick Share is still faster for moving photos or videos, but PlainApp is more versatile for browsing and organizing the rest of your phone's contents.
152623e56e8c.summary: PlainApp, a free open-source Android app, lets you browse and manage your phone from a PC browser over Wi-Fi, with no account or PC software. Engadget says Quick Share is faster for transfers, though.
152623e56e8c.pixel_take: A free app that skips accounts, subscriptions and PC installs? In 2026 that's practically a unicorn, though this one still makes you click past a browser warning first.
152623e56e8c.why_it_matters: Many phone-to-PC tools push subscriptions or require software on both devices, so a free, open-source alternative can save money and clutter. It also shows how far browser-based tools can go without dedicated desktop apps.
key_points: PlainApp is free and open source, needs no account, and requires no software on the PC.
It works over the same Wi-Fi via a browser and supports Android 9 or newer.
Remote control didn't work for the reviewer, and Quick Share remains faster for file transfers.

fbe9ad59c54d.headline: Bessent Likens Bank Tech Outages to Vaccine Side Effects: Sore Arm, Safer System
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday appeared to compare a recent wave of technology outages at major U.S. banks to the temporary side effects of vaccines, according to The Hill. His argument: disruptions tied to cybersecurity updates are a small price to pay for stronger protection.

The framing suggests the administration sees the glitches as a byproduct of banks hardening their systems rather than a sign of deeper trouble. Only the headline and teaser were available, so details such as which banks were affected, how long outages lasted, and what specific updates were involved are not covered here.

The vaccine analogy has an intuitive logic. Security patches and system upgrades often require downtime or can cause unexpected glitches, and a brief inconvenience can be better than a successful cyberattack on financial infrastructure. Banks run on sprawling, aging and interconnected software, so changes can ripple in unexpected ways.

Still, customers tend to be less forgiving than patients with a sore arm. When a banking app freezes or a payment stalls, people can miss bills, lose access to cash or simply lose trust. Regulators and lawmakers often press banks on how well they test updates and how quickly they restore service.

The remark also highlights a tension in financial policy: security and reliability both matter, and the two can pull against each other in the short run. How banks communicate about outages, and how fast they fix them, will likely shape whether the vaccine comparison lands or is seen as a shrug from Washington.
fbe9ad59c54d.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that recent bank tech outages are like vaccine side effects, a minor cost of cybersecurity updates, according to The Hill.
fbe9ad59c54d.pixel_take: Nobody wants a lollipop and a lecture when their banking app is down. But a sore arm beats catching a cyberattack, which is presumably the point.
fbe9ad59c54d.why_it_matters: Bank outages affect everyday money access, from paying bills to moving cash. Cybersecurity upgrades protect the financial system, but frequent disruptions can erode customer trust and invite regulatory scrutiny.
key_points: Bessent compared bank tech outages to temporary vaccine side effects.
He argued cybersecurity-related disruptions are a small price for protection.
The remarks were reported by The Hill on Sunday; details of the outages were not provided.

a5b831f26837.headline: Mexico Takes Down Several Drug Kingpins, and Experts Wonder if a New Chapter Is Starting

The material available is limited: the Times frames it as a question, asking whether Mexico is stepping up in the war on drugs. The teaser does not name the kingpins, the cartels involved, or the operations that brought them down, so those details are not reported here.

What the teaser does make clear is the cautious tone. The word is "may," not "has." Experts see a possible turning point, not a confirmed one. Past crackdowns on top cartel leaders have often been followed by splintering groups and fresh power struggles, so a high-profile arrest is not the same as a lasting win.

The context matters beyond Mexico's borders. Mexico is one of the largest trading partners of the United States, and the drug trade has long been a source of tension between the two countries, touching on security, migration and trade policy. Any real change in how Mexico confronts cartels could ripple into those wider relationships.

For now, the story is a signal worth watching rather than a verdict. Whether these takedowns reflect a deeper strategic shift or a string of notable results remains the open question that experts are weighing.

438acf5edc56.headline: Pediatrician Annie Andrews Stuns South Carolina by Beating Senator Darline Graham, Per NYT
body: Annie Andrews, a pediatrician with a taste for blunt talk, pulled off one of the biggest surprises of the midterm elections by defeating Senator Darline Graham in South Carolina, according to The New York Times.

The Times' framing is a question: is Andrews too real for the Senate? The paper notes she once compared JD Vance to the herpes virus. That is not the usual vocabulary of Senate hopefuls, who tend to sand every sentence down until it can't offend a houseplant.

The material available is limited to the headline and teaser, so details such as the vote margin, turnout and the campaign's key moments are not covered here. Treat this as a first look, not the full postmortem.

Even so, the outline is clear. A first-time style challenger with a medical background and a habit of saying what she thinks beat an incumbent in a contest the Times calls one of the most shocking upsets of the cycle. Voters, it seems, were willing to gamble on someone who sounds like a person rather than a press release.

The next test is whether that style survives contact with Washington, where committee hearings, party leaders and cable news reward caution. South Carolinians chose her, and now they will watch whether plain speech becomes a strength or a liability once she holds the office.
438acf5edc56.summary: Pediatrician Annie Andrews defeated Senator Darline Graham in South Carolina, a major midterm upset, according to The New York Times, which asks whether her blunt style will work in the Senate.

2e34b198714b.headline: Eric Trump-backed robot startup's staff lose health benefits as cash runs dry
body: Employees at Foundation Future Industries, a humanoid robot startup advised and backed by Eric Trump, were told on a Friday evening that their health benefits through administrator Rippling have been terminated, according to a memo obtained by CNBC. The San Francisco company is also waiting on a possible $150 million investment from South Korea's Base Group.

The memo said staff would be offered COBRA, the federal program that lets workers keep their insurance by paying the full premium themselves. A Foundation HR manager wrote that the last pay run through Rippling was in October, so benefits ended retroactive to that month. The company said it would reimburse COBRA premiums and was onboarding a new benefits provider.

Rippling told CNBC the cause was Foundation's own unpaid bills. It said a client unable to meet payroll and benefits obligations for multiple months gets a warning and is then terminated. Some employees, especially those with family members in medical treatment, fear the company may not have the money to reimburse them, people with direct knowledge told CNBC.

Staff were last paid on Oct. 15, and the next payday on Nov. 30 would be a third straight cycle without income. Many are burning through savings and interviewing elsewhere, and office attendance has dropped sharply, according to people familiar. CNBC earlier reported that some employees are angry about a $4.6 million loan co-founder Sankaet Pathak took from the company last year. Pathak reportedly defended it by saying he had invested his own money and takes a nominal salary.

Foundation is seeking a bridge loan from three or four venture firms, including investor Tribe Capital, to hold out until the Base Group money, which Pathak says could land in December or January. Base told Reuters it is considering an investment, but nothing is final. People familiar also said HR warned that employees filing wage complaints with California would be dismissed, and that Pathak floated offering equity to keep staff. Base paid the Trump Organization $2 million in 2025, according to the New York Times, which drew scrutiny from Democratic senators. Foundation, Tribe and Eric Trump did not immediately comment.
2e34b198714b.summary: Staff at Eric Trump-backed Foundation Future Industries lost health benefits after missed payrolls, per CNBC. The robot startup is chasing a bridge loan while awaiting a possible $150 million investment from South Korea's Base Group.
2e34b198714b.why_it_matters: The episode shows how quickly a hyped robotics startup can run into trouble when funding stalls, and how workers bear the risk first. It also shows how much a single unconfirmed investment can matter to a company's survival.
key_points: Foundation employees lost Rippling health benefits retroactive to October and were offered COBRA.
Staff were last paid Oct. 15 and face a third missed pay cycle on Nov. 30.
The company is seeking a bridge loan while awaiting a possible, unconfirmed $150 million from Base Group.

05a5742bcea1.headline: Starlink in 2020 vs. 2026: Cheaper Monthly Bills, But Your Mileage (and ZIP Code) May Vary
body: Starlink's cheapest US home plan now costs $55 a month, which is $44 less than the $99 monthly fee in the October 2020 public beta, according to Engadget. That works out to $528 a year in savings on the subscription alone, though the full picture is messier.

The 2020 launch was branded the "Better Than Nothing Beta," and it was refreshingly honest. Customers were told to expect download speeds of 50 to 150 Mbps, latency of 20 to 40ms and the occasional stretch of no connection at all. The $499 hardware kit included the original round dish, a mounting tripod and a Wi-Fi router. Add the first $99 payment and the opening bill was $598, before shipping and taxes. A full first year at that rate would have run $1,687 including equipment.

Prices then wandered upward. SpaceX raised the monthly rate to $110 in March 2022, with existing users hit in April, and blamed inflation. Hardware rose to $599 for new customers and $549 for those with existing deposits. By 2023, pricing depended on location: $90 where network capacity was spare and $120 where it was tight.

Today there are three main residential plans: Residential 100 Mbps at $55, Residential 200 Mbps at $85 and Residential Max at $130. All offer unlimited data, but the first two have speed caps. Max gets higher network priority and claims speeds of 400 Mbps or more in suitable conditions. In select areas, the equipment can be rented with no upfront cost, which lowers the barrier to entry but changes the ownership picture. SpaceX also raised residential rates in 2026, though the entry-level price is still below its 2020 level.

Engadget notes that discounts and demand-based regional pricing mean two neighbors in different places could pay very different bills for the same service. Starlink can cost more than cable, fiber or 5G home internet, but its value is availability for people stuck with slow DSL or unreliable cellular. The portable Roam plan costs $55 for 100GB of high-speed data, while Roam Unlimited is $175 a month.
05a5742bcea1.summary: Starlink's entry home plan is $55 a month in 2026, $44 below the 2020 beta price. But rate hikes, regional pricing, discounts and equipment rentals mean what customers actually pay can differ widely.
05a5742bcea1.pixel_take: Starlink went from "Better Than Nothing" to a menu of tiers, and the price now depends on where you live. Space internet has finally discovered the airline model, minus the legroom jokes.
05a5742bcea1.why_it_matters: Satellite internet is a real alternative for people without good fiber or cable, so its pricing shapes household budgets in underserved areas. Demand-based regional rates and rental options show how SpaceX balances limited network capacity against growth, which matters for anyone comparing home internet costs.
key_points: Entry plan is $55 a month in 2026 versus $99 in the 2020 beta, a $44 monthly drop.
Hardware cost $499 in 2020; some areas now offer no-upfront equipment rentals.
Current plans run $55, $85 and $130 monthly, with Roam options at $55 and $175.

83c8a30ff39a.headline: Albanese's Office Now Outnumbers the Entire Crossbench's Extra Staff, Integrity Report Finds
body: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has handed himself more political staff, and paid them more, than his predecessors, while the crossbench got fewer extras, according to a Centre for Public Integrity report cited by AAP via The Guardian's live politics coverage.

The report looks at political staffing allocations over 13 years and describes a top-heavy prime minister's office. Of Albanese's current 59 political staff, three-quarters are classed as senior, up from 61% when he took office. Under Tony Abbott, senior staff were under half of the team.
Pay is part of the picture. Senior staff salaries range from $156,510 to $317,152 a year, not counting travel and other allowances, while non-senior staff top out at $167,530.

The office has also grown in size. It had 51 staff at the 2022 election, peaked at 65 before the 2025 election, and has since settled at 59. That is more than the whole crossbench combined: the Greens have 17 extra staff, One Nation five, and 17 independents (including one-person parties) share 30 extra staff in total.

These political staff sit on top of the standard electorate officers every MP and senator receives, and both their numbers and pay bands are set at the prime minister's discretion. Asked about it at a press conference, Albanese said it was not a system he created but one he inherited, adding that his government increased staffing for every member of the House of Representatives and the Senate.
83c8a30ff39a.summary: A Centre for Public Integrity report says Albanese's 59-strong political staff is the most senior-heavy yet and outnumbers the crossbench's extra staff combined. Albanese says he inherited the system.
83c8a30ff39a.pixel_take: When the boss sets the headcount, the pay bands and the rules, the org chart tends to grow upward. Even the crossbench's 30 extra staff can't out-vote a 59-person office.
83c8a30ff39a.why_it_matters: Political staffing is paid for by taxpayers, so who gets resources shapes how much scrutiny a government faces. A larger, better-paid prime ministerial team against a thinner crossbench can tilt the balance of influence in Parliament.
key_points: Albanese's office has 59 staff, three-quarters of them senior, up from 61% at the start of his term.
Senior salaries run from $156,510 to $317,152; the crossbench shares 52 extra staff in total.
Albanese says he inherited the system and raised staffing for every MP and senator.

9ca1323a09e2.headline: Google TV acting sluggish? Clear the cache before you hurl the remote
body: If your Google TV has started stuttering like a presenter without slides, Engadget has a troubleshooting guide that starts with clearing the cache. It is a simple first step for slow performance, app crashes and general glitches, though the outlet stresses it is not a cure-all.

A cache stores data, such as TV show thumbnails, so apps can pull it up quickly later. Google TV manages these caches automatically, but according to Engadget they can still swell or get corrupted, especially if you have lots of apps installed or large video files stored. Storage is tight on these devices: the Google TV Streamer, which replaced the Chromecast, has 32GB, the bare minimum for an Android device.

There are two routes. For system-wide problems, open Settings from the home screen, then go to System, Storage, Internal shared storage and Cached data, and confirm with OK to wipe the cache for all apps. If only one app misbehaves, go to Settings, Apps, See all apps, pick the culprit, choose Force Stop, then Clear Cache, confirming each time.
If that fails, try the system-wide clear, then reboot the device. As a last resort, clear both the app's cache and its data, which resets it to its default state, so you will have to set it up again.

The bigger point is that a cache clear is a short-term patch for a deeper problem: not enough storage. Engadget advises keeping roughly 10 percent of an Android device's storage free. After clearing the cache, check the storage screen, and if 90 percent or more is full, start deleting.

Back up and remove big media files first, but for most Google TVs the real hog is installed apps. Start by dumping those you have not touched in ages, like the streaming service you grabbed to watch a single movie.
9ca1323a09e2.summary: Engadget explains how to clear the cache on Google TV, system-wide or per app, and warns it is only a stopgap if storage is nearly full. Keeping about 10 percent free is advised.
9ca1323a09e2.pixel_take: Your TV has 32GB and you installed 40 streaming apps for one movie each. The cache isn't the problem; your digital hoarding is.
9ca1323a09e2.why_it_matters: Streaming boxes ship with little storage, so slowdowns are common and fixing them costs nothing compared with buying new hardware. Knowing basic maintenance can extend a device's useful life and save you money.
key_points: Clear the cache system-wide via Settings > System > Storage, or per app via Settings > Apps.
The Google TV Streamer has only 32GB, so caches and apps fill it fast.
Keep about 10 percent of storage free and delete unused apps if 90 percent is full.
