c32e65acfc49.headline: CrowdStrike Agrees to Buy Zscaler in $43.9 Billion All-Stock Cybersecurity Mega-Merger
body: CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at $43.9 billion, the two companies announced on Monday, according to TechCrunch. It is a blockbuster pairing in the cybersecurity world, and it is aimed squarely at the AI era.

Zscaler, based in San Jose, California, sells cloud security products to about 8,000 enterprise customers. Its specialty is zero-trust technology, which makes employees prove who they are every single time they access an internal system or resource. The idea is that a hacker holding stolen credentials still cannot wander freely around a company's network.

CrowdStrike comes at the problem from a different angle. It protects the computers, laptops, phones and other devices connected to a company's network. The companies say that merging its endpoint protection software with Zscaler's zero-trust platform will give customers "superior protection" against data breaches.

The pitch also leans heavily on artificial intelligence. The companies said the combination will create the "largest single addressable market" in cybersecurity and help customers adopt AI safely, a theme that is hard to avoid in any tech announcement these days.

The deal still needs regulatory approval and is expected to close around this time next year. Because it is paid in stock rather than cash, the transaction depends on the value of CrowdStrike's shares, and regulators will decide whether combining two big security vendors raises competition concerns.
c32e65acfc49.summary: CrowdStrike will buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in stock, combining device protection with zero-trust security. The companies say it will help customers adopt AI safely. Regulatory approval is needed, with closing expected in about a year.
c32e65acfc49.pixel_take: Zero trust meets endpoint protection: the only merger where both sides will presumably ask each other for ID at the door, every single time.
c32e65acfc49.why_it_matters: A deal of this size signals that companies are consolidating security vendors as AI changes how businesses handle data and access. Investors in cybersecurity stocks should watch regulators and CrowdStrike's share price, since the all-stock structure ties the deal's value to the market. Enterprise customers could see fewer, bigger security platforms to choose from.
key_points: CrowdStrike will buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal worth $43.9 billion.
Zscaler's zero-trust platform serves about 8,000 enterprise customers and will join CrowdStrike's endpoint protection.
The deal needs regulatory approval and is expected to close around this time next year.

512453057e1c.headline: Nvidia soars 30% as Jensen Huang returns as CEO, dragging tech stocks along for the ride
body: Nvidia shares opened up 30% in New York on Monday after the chipmaker reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as chief executive with immediate effect, according to BBC News. The move added roughly $1 trillion to the company's market value.

The reversal is a whiplash one. Less than two weeks earlier, Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and Nvidia's shares had fallen significantly in the interim. The board voted unanimously to bring him back after what the company called a series of discussions and meetings with him.

The rally spread well beyond one company. The tech-heavy Nasdaq was up 6.5% in early trading. Microsoft and Amazon each gained nearly 4%, while Apple rose less than 2%. Other chipmakers did even better: Micron Technology jumped 19%, Intel climbed 14% and AMD gained nearly 7%. Much of the buying began in pre-market trading, before Huang's return was announced, following heavy tech losses on Friday.

Friday was ugly for Nvidia in particular. Its shares fell nearly 14% after Reuters reported, in a claim the BBC has not confirmed, that the US Securities and Exchange Commission was investigating the company's accounting practices. Monday's bounce comes on top of that cloud, not after it has cleared.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage XTB, called Huang the 'godfather' of AI with a 'talismanic influence over the sector'. She noted that although he holds no special voting shares, the directors evidently could not picture the company without him.
Nvidia sits at the center of the AI boom, since its chips are central to the industry. That is why one executive's job status can move not just one stock but a whole corner of the market.
512453057e1c.summary: Nvidia shares jumped 30% after the board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO less than two weeks after he resigned. The Nasdaq rose 6.5% in early trading as chip and tech stocks rallied.
512453057e1c.pixel_take: Two weeks out, one unanimous board vote back in, and a trillion dollars reappears. Most of us can't get a refund on a toaster that fast.
512453057e1c.why_it_matters: Nvidia is so central to the AI trade that a single leadership decision swung the Nasdaq by 6.5% and moved rivals and big tech alike. For anyone with index funds or retirement accounts, it shows how concentrated market performance has become in a few AI-linked names. The reported SEC probe remains an unresolved risk.
key_points: Nvidia opened up 30%, adding about $1 trillion in market value, after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO.
The Nasdaq rose 6.5% early; Micron gained 19%, Intel 14% and AMD nearly 7%.
Shares had fallen nearly 14% Friday on unconfirmed reports of an SEC accounting investigation.

143cfc55d1d6.headline: Your Closed Support Tickets Might Be AI Training Gold, Says a Data-Licensing Startup
body: SourceX, a Los Angeles-based company, is pitching businesses on an idea: the old support tickets, finished projects and documented workflows sitting in their software could be licensed as training and evaluation data for AI, according to a sponsored-style piece published by Digital Trends on November 23, 2026.

The company says it licenses approved operational business data directly from firms. Potential sources include support conversations, documented workflows and internal company knowledge. The argument is that a full record, from the question to the attempted fixes to the final outcome, shows how a business actually solves problems, which is more useful than a pile of disconnected messages.

On the process, SourceX says companies approve the scope and then sign with it, and the firm handles agreements, data preparation, delivery and payment. It describes de-identifying data before use or onward sharing. The material itself cautions that this does not replace a review of privacy, confidentiality and contractual restrictions. An initial fit check requires no record uploads, only a description of the records.

Money is where the fine print matters. SourceX advertises substantial potential payments for large enterprise datasets, but says the upper figure is neither typical nor guaranteed, and that actual deals depend on qualification, dataset fit and signed terms. It also runs a referral program, including an optional bonus of 20% of directly invited partners' eligible paid rewards, one level only. Rewards require qualifying transactions, acceptance, payments and approval, and signups alone earn nothing.

The suggested first step is practical: work out which records your company controls and who is authorized to discuss them. Describing the system, the time period and the kinds of completed work is enough to start. The text frames the key question as whether the archive fits, not how big an export can be.
Readers should note the piece is promotional in nature and carries a disclaimer that it is not legal or financial advice.
143cfc55d1d6.summary: SourceX says companies could license approved records like support tickets and workflows to train AI. It advertises large potential payouts, but stresses they are not typical or guaranteed and depend on qualification and signed terms.
143cfc55d1d6.pixel_take: Your closed tickets finally get a second career. Just make sure legal reads the contract before your 2019 customer rants become a machine's bedtime stories.
143cfc55d1d6.why_it_matters: AI developers need high-quality, real-world data, and that is turning internal company archives into a possible new revenue stream. But privacy, confidentiality and contract risks are real, and advertised payouts are best-case figures, so companies should do legal due diligence before sharing anything.
key_points: SourceX licenses approved business records such as support conversations and workflows for AI training and evaluation.

1cb78417896f.headline: White House says Trump was 'totally involved' in bringing Jensen Huang back as Nvidia CEO
body: The White House is taking a victory lap over Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO. Communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement, first reported by Semafor, that President Donald Trump was "totally involved" and that the board made a great decision, according to The Verge.

Trump repeated the point on CNBC, saying the US has to "protect our geniuses." He said he "believed very strongly" that Huang should return, and claimed that without his involvement Nvidia would have had a very sad stretch ahead.

On the investigation, Trump said it showed Huang had shown bad judgment in what he called somewhat unrelated incidents, but had done nothing wrong. On Truth Social, he wrote that the government has no reason to believe Huang's return poses a national security risk, and that the Attorney General confirmed it has no evidence of unlawful conduct by him.

Nvidia's own announcement points the same way. The company said its board received input from senior levels of the US government that made it confident reinstating Huang would not create a national security risk. That followed reports about Huang's involvement with an alleged Chinese spy.

The timeline adds to the picture. Less than 12 hours before the decision, Trump posted that bringing Huang back would be the best thing for Nvidia and the country, and urged the board to rehire him. Semafor now reports he also called into the board meeting around that time to argue the same case.
It is an unusual spectacle: the head of a government publicly claiming credit for a private company's personnel call, while the company itself cites government input as a reason for the decision.
1cb78417896f.summary: The White House says Trump was 'totally involved' in Nvidia's decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang, and Nvidia says it received input from senior US government levels on national security concerns.
1cb78417896f.pixel_take: Nvidia's board meeting apparently had a surprise guest on the line. Corporate governance, now featuring a very persuasive speakerphone.

key_points: White House and Trump say he was 'totally involved' in Huang's reinstatement.
Nvidia says its board got input from senior US government levels on national security.
Semafor reports Trump called into the board meeting to urge the rehire.

5566b456d1b7.headline: Leaked death certificates reveal Russia's hidden war toll: over 460,000 dead, little ground gained
body: A Guardian analysis of leaked Russian death certificates has produced the most detailed picture yet of Moscow's losses in Ukraine, identifying more than 460,000 war-linked deaths between the February 2022 invasion and September 2026. The data comes from more than 11 million certificates obtained by the Belarusian-linked Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian hacker collective Silent Crow.

The records, compiled by Russia's statistics agency Rosstat, show a war growing steadily deadlier. Almost 20,000 deaths were logged in the first year and 50,000 in 2023. The toll then topped 134,000 in 2024 and rose a further 52% in 2025 to close to 200,000, or about 548 men a day, against an average of roughly 277 since the start. Russia's defence ministry last updated its official figure in September 2022, at 5,937.

The scale dwarfs recent comparisons, according to the Guardian. About 15,000 Soviet soldiers died over nine years in Afghanistan. In one week from 5 May 2025, Russia lost more men than the US did in eight years in Iraq. In 2025, war became the leading cause of death for Russian men under 65, cited in 29% of certificates with a recorded cause.

The payoff on the map has been thin. Since the start of 2023 Russia has gained about 8,000 sq km, under 1.5% of Ukraine, according to DeepState. Nearly 116,000 deaths with a known location were in Pokrovsk district. After Avdiivka fell, about 88,700 Russian soldiers were recorded as dying there while troops advanced 39km, more than 2,200 per kilometre.

Analysts say the losses are biting. Janis Kluge of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs said falling recruitment combined with heavy losses apparently forced Russia to slow attacks in 2026. The average age at death has risen from 34 to nearly 40, as the Kremlin leans on cash bonuses rather than a second unpopular mobilisation. The true toll is probably higher, since missing soldiers are often registered months or years later.
5566b456d1b7.summary: Leaked death certificates analysed by the Guardian show more than 460,000 war-linked Russian deaths since 2022, peaking in 2025, while territorial gains stayed small and the losses deepen Russia's demographic and manpower problems.
5566b456d1b7.why_it_matters: Heavy losses and a shrinking pool of recruits strain Russia's labour market, budget and long-term demographics, all of which shape the war's duration and the outlook for sanctions, energy markets and European security spending.
key_points: Guardian analysis found over 460,000 war-linked Russian deaths from February 2022 to September 2026.
2025 was deadliest, with close to 200,000 deaths, about 548 a day.
Russia gained about 8,000 sq km since 2023, under 1.5% of Ukraine, per DeepState.

Stories like this are a reminder that local emergency services often do double duty. Crews trained for fires and accidents regularly step in for animals, and the public tends to cheer when it ends well. The headline's wording, which says the cat was rescued, points to a happy outcome.

93b5534af2ec.headline: Bitcoin bounces back above $63,000 after a liquidation-fueled tumble
body: Bitcoin climbed back above the $63,000 mark after a selloff driven by liquidations, according to Investing.com, which reported the rebound on November 23, 2026.

The source material is thin on details, so the exact size and timing of the drop are not available here. What the headline does make clear is the mechanism: the slide was tied to liquidations rather than a single named piece of news.

Liquidations happen when traders who borrowed money to bet on price moves are forced to close their positions because their collateral no longer covers the loan. When prices fall quickly, those forced sales can push prices lower still, which triggers more liquidations. It is a bit like a domino rally where the dominoes are leveraged bets.

The flip side is that such selloffs can reverse quickly once the forced selling runs out, since the drop reflects mechanics more than a change in long-term views. A rebound above $63,000 suggests buyers stepped in after the shakeout, though one bounce does not tell us whether the move will last.
For anyone watching crypto, the episode is a reminder that leverage amplifies volatility in both directions, and that sharp daily swings can say more about positioning than about fundamentals.
93b5534af2ec.summary: Bitcoin recovered above $63,000 following a selloff driven by liquidations, Investing.com reported. The rebound shows how forced selling can exaggerate swings in both directions.
93b5534af2ec.pixel_take: Leveraged traders got a lesson in gravity, then bitcoin remembered it has a trampoline. Borrowed conviction, it turns out, is the most fragile kind.
93b5534af2ec.why_it_matters: Liquidation-driven moves show how much leverage shapes crypto prices, so headline swings may reflect forced trades rather than new fundamentals. For investors, that means volatility risk is real, especially when borrowing is involved.
key_points: Bitcoin rebounded above $63,000, per Investing.com.
The preceding selloff was driven by liquidations.
Forced selling from leveraged bets can magnify moves both ways.

b29106e08869.headline: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO and Stocks Jump, With Wall Street Already Halfway to Cheerful
body: Nvidia's board has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, and the news sent the chipmaker's shares soaring on Monday, according to The New York Times. The announcement landed as U.S. markets were already leaning higher.

Before the Nvidia headline, the S&P 500 was set to rise on Monday, recovering from a sharp fall the week before. In other words, the market had already put on its good shoes, and the Huang news handed it a jetpack.

The material available does not explain the circumstances of Mr. Huang's departure or the reasons for his return, so those details remain unclear. What is clear is the reaction: investors treated the reinstatement as good news for Nvidia, and the stock moved sharply on it.

The reaction shows how closely a company's valuation can be tied to its leader. Nvidia is one of the most closely watched companies in the market, and a founder-style chief executive often carries a premium in investors' minds. When leadership looks uncertain, shares tend to reflect that. When certainty returns, they can rebound quickly.

It also matters beyond one company. Large, heavily weighted stocks can move major indexes like the S&P 500, so a big swing in Nvidia can ripple into retirement accounts, index funds and the broader mood on Wall Street. Monday's rise followed a rough prior week, and the Nvidia news added momentum to a market already trying to recover.
b29106e08869.summary: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, sending the company's shares soaring on Monday as the S&P 500 was already poised to rebound from last week's sharp fall, The New York Times reported.
b29106e08869.pixel_take: Nothing calms a market like the boss coming back. Wall Street was already cheering for a rebound, and Nvidia just handed it the confetti cannon.
b29106e08869.why_it_matters: Nvidia is a heavyweight in major indexes, so its swings can move portfolios and index funds far beyond tech investors. The reaction shows how much markets price in leadership stability. For ordinary savers, one stock's jump can quietly shape the broader market's mood.
key_points: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, per The New York Times.
Nvidia shares soared on the news on Monday.
The S&P 500 was already set to rise after a sharp fall last week.

163a5367dcf2.headline: China Says It Swapped a Damaged Oil Well Casing Nearly 6,000 Feet Down, a Claimed Record
body: Xinjiang Oilfield, a unit of China National Petroleum Corp. (CNPC), says it has replaced a damaged well casing at a depth of nearly 6,000 feet, a feat it describes as a record, according to Interesting Engineering.

The details are thin. The source material available to us includes the headline and a short teaser, but no technical specifics on how the repair was carried out, how long it took, or what it cost. We also cannot independently verify the record claim, so it should be read as the company's own description.

For non-specialists, a casing is the steel pipe lining an oil well. It keeps the borehole from collapsing, seals off different rock layers and stops fluids from leaking where they shouldn't. When it gets damaged, the usual options are costly: patch it, plug the well, or drill a new one.

Swapping out a casing section at depth, rather than abandoning the well, is the kind of work that can extend the life of an aging field. If the claim holds up, it suggests Chinese operators are pushing workover technology, the repair and maintenance side of the oil business that rarely makes headlines but matters a lot to margins.

Neither the source text nor the teaser says whether the technique will be used more widely or offered commercially. Until CNPC or independent experts provide more detail, the record remains an announcement rather than a verified benchmark.
163a5367dcf2.summary: Xinjiang Oilfield, part of CNPC, reports replacing a damaged well casing at nearly 6,000 feet and calls it a record, per Interesting Engineering. Technical details and independent verification are not yet available.
163a5367dcf2.pixel_take: Fixing a pipe is hard enough under the sink. Doing it almost 6,000 feet underground and calling it a record is the ultimate plumber flex.
163a5367dcf2.why_it_matters: Repairing old wells instead of drilling new ones can cut costs and keep output flowing from mature fields. For energy markets, small gains in well longevity add up across thousands of wells. It also shows where national oil companies are investing engineering effort.

The company calls it a record, but the claim has not been independently verified.

9ae3fa8ff2a7.headline: AirPods Pro 3 hit $149, the same price as the weaker AirPods 5
body: Apple's AirPods Pro 3 have fallen to $149 at Amazon and Walmart as of Monday morning, according to The Verge. That is $100 below the $249 list price, a 40 percent discount, and it lands just ahead of Black Friday.

The Verge says it is the lowest price yet for Apple's newest flagship earbuds. They have usually sold for around $199 outside big deal events, and the previous best the outlet had tracked was $169, which is what Best Buy currently charges.

The odd part is the lineup. At $149, the Pro 3 cost the same as the newer AirPods 5 with the wireless charging case, which The Verge calls less impressive. In other words, the premium model is temporarily priced like the budget-minded one.

On features, The Verge describes the Pro 3 as Apple's best-sounding and longest-lasting AirPods, and they come with five silicone ear tips. Compared with the second-generation AirPods Pro, they offer better water resistance (IP57 versus IP54) and longer battery life per charge (eight hours versus six). Noise cancellation is improved too, and built-in sensors can track heart rate. The case also carries Apple's second-generation Ultra Wideband chip.

Prices at big retailers can move quickly during sales season, and the $149 figure applies to the retailers named above. If you were eyeing either pair, the Pro 3 look like the stronger buy at this price, per The Verge.
9ae3fa8ff2a7.summary: The AirPods Pro 3 dropped to $149 at Amazon and Walmart, 40 percent off their $249 list price. That matches the price of the AirPods 5, a less capable model, according to The Verge.
9ae3fa8ff2a7.pixel_take: Apple's pricing ladder just tripped: the fancy earbuds now cost the same as the lesser ones. Black Friday, where the premium seat gets sold at economy fares.
9ae3fa8ff2a7.why_it_matters: Early Black Friday cuts on flagship gadgets show how aggressively retailers compete for holiday spending. When a premium product matches a cheaper model's price, shoppers get more for the same money, and the cheaper model may be pressured to follow.
key_points: AirPods Pro 3 are $149 at Amazon and Walmart, down from $249.
Best Buy sells them for $169, the previous lowest price The Verge had seen.
At $149 they match the AirPods 5 with wireless charging case.

a7098c5bfccf.headline: Trump to Hit Back at Newsom's Mass Commutation of Death Row Sentences in DOJ Remarks
body: President Donald Trump is set to criticize California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) over his decision to commute the sentences of more than 548 inmates who were facing execution, according to The Hill. Trump is expected to make the remarks at the Justice Department on Monday afternoon.

The report, based on a teaser of the story, says the president will push back on the governor's move. The full text of his planned comments was not available, so the specific arguments he intends to make are not yet clear.

The setting is notable. The Justice Department is the federal government's top law enforcement body, and choosing it as the venue signals that the administration wants to frame the issue as a matter of crime and punishment, not just a state-level policy dispute.

The clash also adds another chapter to the long-running political sparring between Trump and Newsom, two high-profile figures from opposing parties. Capital punishment has long been a divisive issue in American politics, with supporters pointing to accountability for the worst crimes and opponents citing cost, error risk and moral concerns.

Commutation is a power governors hold to reduce a sentence without erasing a conviction. In general terms, it means inmates who had been condemned would no longer face execution, though the specifics of their new sentences were not detailed in the material available.
a7098c5bfccf.summary: Trump will criticize California Gov. Gavin Newsom's commutation of more than 548 death row sentences in remarks at the Justice Department on Monday, according to The Hill.
a7098c5bfccf.why_it_matters: Fights over criminal justice shape political agendas, state budgets and federal-state relations. A high-profile clash between the White House and California's governor can influence policy debates and voter attention heading into future elections.

Remarks are scheduled for Monday afternoon at the Justice Department.

The dollar reserve is also worth a note. Companies hold cash reserves to cover obligations and give themselves flexibility. Authorizing up to $1 billion to move out of that reserve suggests Strategy is willing to use its cash cushion actively, though the exact plans were not detailed in the teaser.

28fb1e929b99.headline: Netanyahu Pushes to Strike Iran Again: Security Need or Political Survival Play?
body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is making the case for renewed strikes on Iran, according to The New York Times, framing the move as a matter of national security. The question now being asked in Israel is whether the plan serves the country, or the man who leads it.

Netanyahu's position is straightforward: in his telling, renewed military action is about protecting Israel. That is the familiar language of any government weighing force against a long-standing adversary, and it carries real weight with many voters.

But the Times reports that military analysts and opposition leaders see it differently. Their argument is that the prime minister is putting his own interests first, which is a pointed accusation in a country where decisions about war are meant to rise above personal politics.

The material available does not spell out the specific evidence either side relies on, so the details of the military case and the political critique remain unclear. What is clear is the shape of the dispute: an official security rationale on one side, and skeptics from both the defense establishment and the opposition on the other.

Why does this tension matter beyond Israel? Any renewed strikes involving Iran tend to ripple outward, because the region is central to energy supply and global risk sentiment. Whether a leader's motives are strategic or personal also shapes how much trust allies, markets and his own public place in the decision.
28fb1e929b99.summary: Netanyahu calls renewed strikes on Iran a national security necessity, but military analysts and opposition leaders told The New York Times he may be putting his own interests first.

f922f5d9cdd0.headline: Roku Remote Blinking Green? Don't Panic, It's Usually Just Hungry for Batteries
body: A flashing green light on a Roku remote usually points to low batteries or a pairing process, not a catastrophe, according to a new Engadget explainer published on November 23, 2026. Only in one scenario does it mean the remote is likely toast.

Roku has a big footprint in smart TVs. Models from TCL and Hisense ship with Roku OS built in, and it is the main option for brands that skip Google TV, Fire TV or their own software. That makes a mysteriously blinking remote a widely shared annoyance.

The most common cause is weak power. If your remote takes replaceable batteries, swap them out. Engadget notes Roku recommends alkaline batteries for those models, and that frequent low-battery warnings may mean you are using rechargeables. Remotes with a built-in battery need a recharge. You can check battery levels under Settings, Remotes & devices, Remotes, then your remote and About.

The light also appears when you set up a replacement remote or trigger the physical pairing controls, which means holding a dedicated button, or Back and Home together, for five seconds. That blinking is normal. The red flag is rapid flashing after you have re-paired the remote, which suggests it is probably broken and needs replacing. Engadget says official Roku remotes tend to offer better support and features than third-party ones, but check compatibility with your TV or streamer either way.

Before buying, try a restart. With replaceable batteries, remove them, press any two buttons, then reinsert the batteries negative sides first. With a built-in battery, hold the pairing controls for 20 seconds. Resetting the whole Roku is a last resort, wipes your setup, and is unlikely to fix a green-light issue because that is typically about power or pairing rather than software.

If all else fails, your phone can step in. The Roku app works as a backup, and AirPlay from an iPhone or MacBook, or screen mirroring from an Android phone, can often get your content on screen directly.
f922f5d9cdd0.summary: A flashing green light on a Roku remote usually means low batteries or pairing, per Engadget. Rapid flashing after re-pairing suggests a broken remote. Restarting it or using your phone are easy workarounds.
f922f5d9cdd0.pixel_take: A blinking green light that just wants fresh batteries: the only relationship in your living room that asks for so little and still gets ignored for weeks.
f922f5d9cdd0.why_it_matters: Smart TV platforms like Roku are in millions of homes, so small hardware quirks become everyday household costs. Knowing a fix may be a few batteries can save you from buying an unneeded replacement remote.
key_points: Green flashing usually means low battery or active pairing.
Rapid flashing after re-pairing likely signals a broken remote.
Restarting the remote or using the Roku app are easy fixes.

46132fec3248.headline: Markets are doing the tech-stock tango: here's what to do before you hit the panic button
body: Global stock markets have had a wild ride, with sharp rallies followed by painful sell-offs as investors grow nervous about the valuations of AI and technology companies, according to The Guardian. Last week, markets tumbled worldwide on Friday and the US Nasdaq closed 5% below its 1 January level.

The turbulence has had plenty of plot twists. AI company Anthropic had a record-breaking first day on the market last week. Earlier this month, the surprisingly large Democratic win in the US midterms was followed by the exit of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang over an alleged relationship with a Chinese spy. On Monday, his dramatic return sent Nvidia shares soaring and helped lift US markets.

Why does this hit ordinary savers? Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, says global equity funds and S&P 500 trackers are among the most popular passive investments, and both lean heavily on tech giants. US shares now make up 73% of the MSCI World index, up from about half 15 years ago. Tech officially accounts for 30%, or roughly 35% once Alphabet and Meta are counted. A global fund may be less diversified than it looks.

The first piece of advice from the experts is to stay calm. Losses are only locked in when you sell, and many investors are still sitting on gains: the FTSE 100 is above last year's level, and Scottish Mortgage is still well up year on year despite falling since mid-October. Holly Mackay of Boring Money says the instinct to act is often the worst response. Coatsworth notes markets have bounced back from past shocks, including the April 2025 tariff drop, inflation and Covid.

Still, it is a good moment for a check-up. Camilla Esmund of interactive investor suggests spreading risk across sectors, regions and asset classes, and those nearing retirement should check their holdings fit their plan for drawing income. To trim tech exposure, Coatsworth points to a global fund excluding the US, though that means missing out if the likes of Nvidia rebound. A middle path is an equal-weight global ETF, where the US share was 40.6% at the end of September.

Some see opportunity. Hargreaves Lansdown said clients bought overseas tech shares after the post-midterm falls, and Mackay says she is sitting tight and may buy quality companies she thinks are unfairly punished.
46132fec3248.summary: Tech and AI jitters have shaken global markets. Experts quoted by The Guardian urge savers not to panic-sell, but to review diversification, especially given how tech-heavy global tracker funds have become.
46132fec3248.pixel_take: Your 'diversified' global fund turns out to be a tech fund wearing a world map as a costume. Nice disguise, but the Nasdaq saw right through it.
46132fec3248.why_it_matters: Pensions and index funds hold large stakes in a handful of tech giants, so AI-driven swings reach far beyond day traders. Knowing how concentrated your portfolio is helps you avoid panic decisions that lock in losses.
key_points: Nasdaq closed 5% below its 1 January level after Friday's global sell-off.
US stocks are 73% of the MSCI World index, with tech about 35% including Alphabet and Meta.
Experts advise against panic selling and suggest reviewing diversification and risk.

eee8e7bbee50.headline: AI agents are swiping credit cards, and crypto wonders if it got left on read
body: AI agents are already using credit cards to make transactions, according to Cointelegraph, and that is raising a pointed question for the crypto industry: where does digital money fit in an emerging agent economy?

The material available is thin on specifics, so details such as which agents, which card networks or how much money is involved are not known here. What the report does establish is the basic tension. Software that can shop, book and pay on its own is not a future concept; it is already leaning on the old plastic rails.

That matters because crypto has long pitched itself as the natural currency for machines. Blockchains run around the clock, settle without a bank's office hours and do not need a human to fill in a billing address. In theory, a bot should feel more at home there than at a checkout page designed for people.

Yet the report suggests that in practice, agents are reaching for the thing that already works almost everywhere: the credit card. Merchants accept it, consumers trust it and consumer protections such as dispute processes are built around it. Incumbency, as usual, is a powerful feature.

None of this settles the contest. Cards and crypto could end up serving different jobs in the agent economy, or one could absorb the strengths of the other. For now, the headline question is open, and the bots seem to be doing their shopping the familiar way.
eee8e7bbee50.summary: Cointelegraph reports AI agents are already paying with credit cards, prompting questions about whether crypto, long pitched as machine-friendly money, will find a role in the emerging agent economy.
eee8e7bbee50.pixel_take: Crypto spent years building money for robots, and the robots walked straight past it to use a credit card. Somewhere, a very patient blockchain is checking its messages.
eee8e7bbee50.why_it_matters: If autonomous software becomes a major source of purchases, the payment rails it picks could decide who captures the fees and growth. Card networks have a head start, while crypto must prove it offers something agents and merchants actually need.

The trend raises questions about crypto's place in the agent economy.

For readers watching their wallets, the stakes are indirect but real. Whether big bills on taxes, spending, regulation or technology need 60 votes shapes how fast, and how drastically, policy can change.

e98ce263e496.headline: West Bank 'closed military zones' are turning into settler land, Palestinians and rights groups say
body: Closed military zones across the occupied West Bank are increasingly being used by Israeli settlers to take over land, while Palestinian owners are kept out, according to an Al Jazeera report published on November 23, 2026. Villagers, lawyers and monitoring groups describe a pattern in which orders that formally bar everyone without a permit are enforced mainly against Palestinians.

In Deir Abu Mishal, west of Ramallah, farmer Saleh Zahran said he could not reach his family's 120 olive trees for five months after settlers set up an outpost about 1km away in June. A High Court decision on November 10 granted two days of army-coordinated harvesting. His lawyer, Ghiyath Nasser, says villagers could access less than a third of the area, leaving Zahran able to pick about 20 trees. He said his farm room was looted and his saplings had died.

In al-Mughayyir, village council members say about 80 percent of the 43,000 dunams of village land lies behind an eastern entrance that has been closed for years, and villagers can move freely on only about 900 dunams. Yesh Din documents show a closure order issued after the August 2025 clearing of olive trees was renewed several times. The group's legal objection says it is enforced only against owners while settlers graze, plough and build. Lawyer Lior Zur called it selective enforcement that transfers possession from Palestinian owners to settlers.

Dror Etkes of Kerem Navot, which tracks settler land takeovers, said closing an area to Palestinians usually leads to settlers moving in. A July report by Kerem Navot and Peace Now found farm outposts effectively controlled more than 1 million dunams, about 18 percent of the West Bank, at the end of 2025, with roughly 750,000 dunams taken since late 2022.

Lawyers also criticise the courts. In Madama, a petition over an outpost filed in September was given a state response deadline of May 2027. Similar cases were reported in Duma, Burin, Taybeh, Qusra and elsewhere. The report describes unprecedented violence and access restrictions during this olive harvest season. The material did not include an Israeli government response.
e98ce263e496.summary: Al Jazeera reports that closed military zones in the West Bank are being used by settlers to take over land, with orders allegedly enforced mostly against Palestinian owners, according to villagers, lawyers and rights groups.
e98ce263e496.why_it_matters: Land access is the foundation of Palestinian farm income, and many villagers depend on olive harvests for a living. The disputes deepen geopolitical tensions and add to international legal and political pressure on Israel. They also weigh on regional stability, which markets watch closely.
key_points: Villagers say closure orders are enforced against Palestinian owners, not settlers.
A July report found farm outposts control about 18 percent of the West Bank.
Lawyers say court delays and selective enforcement help entrench takeovers.

c0041aadd906.headline: Meta's Gas Supplier Lobbied the EPA Before It Waived Acid Rain Rules for Data Center Plants
body: Williams, a gas power provider to several Meta data centers, met with Environmental Protection Agency officials before the agency recommended exempting data-center power plants from acid rain regulations, according to documents obtained by WIRED. The EPA issued that recommendation in July.

The recommendation covers "islanded" plants, which power data centers directly rather than selling electricity to the grid. The EPA said the Acid Rain Program was built for plants that sell power to the grid, so plants serving only data centers would not need to comply. The agency also said the guidance fits White House orders encouraging developers to build their own power so consumer utility rates don't rise.

Williams was one of three private companies that asked the EPA for guidance. In a February letter, its director of permitting argued that regulatory uncertainty created obstacles for data center development. Calendar invites show executives were invited to at least two EPA meetings, and in an April request Williams called its Ohio and Utah projects "urgent." The EPA said the meetings broadly covered air regulations and that it regularly meets stakeholders.

Williams' materials never named Meta. But the EPA's letter cited an unnamed company building a 500-megawatt gas plant for an adjacent, third-party data center, and Williams' Utah project and two Ohio projects for Meta are each about 500 megawatts. Meta declined to comment, and Williams said it prioritizes environmental protection while seeking to modernize construction timelines.

The pollution math is nuanced. Gas plants emit far less sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides than coal plants. Williams' Utah permit application shows maximums of about 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide a year, versus thousands of tons for a comparable coal plant. The bigger concern is reporting: the program also required carbon dioxide monitoring, so an exemption could mean regulators learn less about data center emissions.

Experts even agree the EPA's reading follows the letter of the law. Joseph Goffman, a former EPA official, and Harvard's Carrie Jenks both say the program was never designed for behind-the-meter generation. Earthjustice and the NRDC disagree and challenged the interpretation in September. With over 110 gigawatts of such gas projects estimated in the US, the stakes are large.
c0041aadd906.summary: Documents show Williams, a gas supplier to Meta data centers, met EPA officials before the agency recommended exempting data-center power plants from acid rain rules. Critics worry about lost emissions reporting.
c0041aadd906.pixel_take: The AI race may be won on speed, but nobody asked what the acid rain thinks. At least the paperwork was marked "urgent."
c0041aadd906.why_it_matters: Cheaper, faster private power plants help AI companies build quickly and may shield consumers from grid-driven rate hikes. But less emissions reporting means less transparency on the environmental cost of the AI boom, a possible regulatory and reputational risk for tech and energy investors.
key_points: Williams, a gas provider for Meta data centers, met EPA officials before the July acid rain exemption recommendation.
The EPA says islanded plants that don't sell to the grid fall outside the Acid Rain Program.
Experts worry the exemption cuts emissions reporting, including CO2, even though gas emits less than coal.

06bff48752d2.headline: Nvidia Stock Rockets 30%-Plus as Jensen Huang Is Reinstated as CEO
body: Nvidia's stock surged more than 30% on Monday, its biggest one-day gain in a decade, after the company made the stunning decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as president and chief executive, according to MarketWatch.

The material available does not spell out the circumstances behind the move, so key details remain unclear, including how the leadership change came about and what the board said. Those details matter, and we will be watching for them as more information emerges.

What the market's reaction does show is how much investors tie Nvidia's value to Huang personally. A gain of this size in a single session is rare for any company, and rarer still for one already worth a great deal. Investors were clearly treating his return as a major event, not a routine management shuffle.

For markets, the jump also underlines how concentrated sentiment around artificial intelligence has become in a handful of names. Nvidia is widely seen as a central player in that trade, so big swings in its shares can ripple through tech indexes and the funds that hold them, including many retirement accounts.

The open question is whether the rally holds. One-day surges driven by leadership news can fade as details emerge and investors turn back to earnings, demand and competition. For now, Monday's trading was a very loud vote of confidence in one executive.
06bff48752d2.summary: Nvidia shares jumped more than 30% on Monday, the biggest gain in a decade, after the company reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO, according to MarketWatch.
06bff48752d2.pixel_take: When a stock rises 30% because one person gets his old job back, that's not a résumé, that's a market-moving boomerang.
06bff48752d2.why_it_matters: Nvidia is a heavyweight in the AI trade, so a move this large can shift tech indexes and portfolios, including index funds many people own. It also shows how much investors can price in a single leader's role.
key_points: Nvidia stock rose more than 30% on Monday, its best day in a decade.
The move followed the decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as president and CEO.
Details behind the leadership change were not available in the source material.

941d9d7c875e.headline: Nvidia Rehires Jensen Huang After 11 Days, and Markets Breathe Again
body: Nvidia's board has reversed course and handed Jensen Huang his job back just 11 days after he left, according to BBC News. His exit followed revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have been a spy for China. Shares in the chipmaker surged on news of his return after a stretch of sharp declines.

The U-turn shows how much the company, and arguably the US market, leans on one person. Nvidia began by making chips for computer game graphics, pivoted to the chips that power AI systems, and now dominates that market. It is one of the world's most valuable firms, and its quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier. Huang led that shift and kept a tight grip, with up to 200 people reporting to him directly.

Part of the worry was Nvidia's role as banker as well as supplier. Through what is called circular financing, it sells chips to customers such as Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, and also lends to or invests in them and other firms in the supply chain. Some investors fear that if Nvidia closed the taps, suppliers might cut spending or jobs, with possible knock-on effects for the wider economy.

Tech figures lobbied hard for his return. Elon Musk claimed critical deals would be lost and backed a 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign, then posted that 'the mistake has been corrected.' Kathleen Brooks of XTB called Huang 'the godfather' of AI and said his return means more of the same on circular financing and AI build-out, which the market loves.

Trump called Huang a 'great patriot and national treasure,' saying the country needs his leadership. Nvidia said it had input from senior US government levels and is confident his reinstatement poses no national security risk.

Still, the rehire does not fix everything. Investors have been rattled by Democratic gains in the midterms, since many campaigned for tougher AI regulation, and doubts persist over whether the huge AI outlay will pay off. Goldman Sachs nonetheless expects AI investment to top $1 trillion in 2026 and to remain the dominant driver of business investment growth next year.
941d9d7c875e.summary: Nvidia's board reinstated CEO Jensen Huang after 11 days, sending shares up. The episode exposed how much the AI boom and US stock market depend on the chipmaker and its web of deals.
941d9d7c875e.pixel_take: Eleven days: barely long enough for a sourdough starter, yet enough to wobble the AI economy. Turns out the board's 'succession plan' was just a very fast undo button.
941d9d7c875e.why_it_matters: Nvidia sits at the center of AI spending that has propped up US stocks, and by extension pensions and investments worldwide. Its habit of financing its own customers means a change in strategy could ripple through the supply chain. Leadership stability here is a market issue, not just a corporate one.
key_points: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang 11 days after his exit, and shares surged.
Nvidia both sells chips to and funds customers like Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, a practice called circular financing.
Goldman Sachs expects AI investment to exceed $1 trillion in 2026 despite lingering doubts and regulation fears.

423071d6f76d.headline: Dutch Privacy Watchdog Tells Shoppers to Skip AI Camera Glasses
body: The Dutch Data Protection Authority is urging consumers not to buy AI-enabled camera glasses, according to TechCrunch. The agency says the internet-connected, always-on wearables compromise the privacy of bystanders and can put their own users at risk.

The statement stops just short of an outright ban. Still, the authority said that using such glasses to record people in public is "almost always prohibited," which is about as close to a red card as a regulator can wave without actually sending anyone off the pitch.

Critics have nicknamed the devices "pervert glasses" because they can be used to film people without permission, particularly to harass women. Some models have a warning light when recording, but privacy advocates argue the signal is not clear enough. Some people have even built phone apps that detect nearby smart-glasses wearers.

The regulator also raised reliability concerns. In one of its tests, a pair of unnamed glasses gave dating advice to an adult who said they were interested in a minor. The same device misread a medicine label and claimed to have called an ambulance when it had not.

The Dutch advice follows Norway, whose government said in September that it was considering a ban on camera-enabled devices. Taken together, the two moves suggest European regulators are starting to look hard at wearables that combine cameras with AI, rather than waiting for the technology to become commonplace.
423071d6f76d.summary: The Dutch data protection authority urged consumers not to buy AI camera glasses, citing bystander privacy, user safety and faulty AI results. Norway is also weighing a ban on camera-enabled devices.
423071d6f76d.pixel_take: Smart glasses that misread medicine labels and fake an ambulance call are less 'the future' and more 'a confident intern wearing your face.' Regulators are right to squint.
423071d6f76d.why_it_matters: Regulatory pushback in Europe could slow the market for AI wearables, which tech companies hope will be the next big consumer device. Compliance costs, restrictions on public recording and reliability concerns could shape what products get sold and how they are designed.
key_points: The Dutch authority says recording people in public with such glasses is almost always prohibited.
Its tests found wrong and unsafe outputs, including a false claim of calling an ambulance.
Norway said in September it was considering a ban on camera-enabled devices.

f571db581dd5.headline: Ukraine Says Its Naval Drones Hit Russian Ships Off Libya, Pushing the War Into the Mediterranean
body: Ukraine has claimed it sank a Russian corvette and hit a Russian cargo vessel off the coast of Libya, a move that stretches the war far from its original battlefield. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the strikes on X on Monday, saying seven Ukrainian-made naval drones were used.

According to Al Jazeera, the corvette Merkury was hit on Sunday at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya, causing an explosion and fire. Satellite imagery showed most of the ship had capsized, with only its bow above water. Zelenskyy said a Russian Ka-27 helicopter was also destroyed, and that the second target, the cargo ship MV Angara, was used to carry weapons and was hit.

The same weekend, the Russian cargo ship Sparta II was struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland, caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters. All 16 crew were evacuated, one with a slight injury. Finland's military assessed Ukraine was likely responsible, while Kyiv has not claimed that attack. Russia said two drones hit the ship in international waters.

Reactions were swift. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called it a "very dangerous trend" and warned of "painful" consequences. Libya's eastern administration condemned a violation of its sovereignty and asked the UN for an international investigation. The rival Tripoli government voiced concern about civilian ports being tied to outside conflicts, and the UN mission in Libya demanded an independent, transparent probe.

The strikes fit a pattern. At least four Russian vessels have reportedly been targeted in November, and earlier incidents include a Russian LNG tanker sunk off Libya in March and an oil tanker hit in the Mediterranean in December 2025. Analyst Alexey Muraviev told Al Jazeera the Mediterranean is now an external theatre of the war, and warned the Gulf of Finland, with Russian and NATO forces nearby, is especially risky.
Muraviev also noted the attacks add risk for global shipping, which already faces security threats around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb.
f571db581dd5.summary: Ukraine says naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury and hit the cargo ship Angara off Libya. Russia warns of consequences, while the UN seeks an investigation and analysts see the war spreading.
f571db581dd5.why_it_matters: Attacks on ships far from Ukraine raise risks for maritime operators and could push up insurance and shipping costs in already tense waters. Any Russia-NATO clash in the Baltic would rattle markets and energy-dependent economies.
key_points: Zelenskyy claims seven naval drones hit the corvette Merkury and cargo ship MV Angara off Libya.
Libya's rival governments and the UN condemned the attacks and called for an investigation.
Analysts warn the war is widening and adding risk to global shipping lanes.

de79ba5ddb88.headline: Trump Dials Into Nvidia Board Meeting, Jensen Huang Gets His Job Back, Shares Jump 34%
body: Nvidia's board voted unanimously on Sunday evening to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, after President Donald Trump personally dialed into a weekend board meeting and pushed for his return, according to Futurism, citing Semafor. Nvidia shares jumped more than 34 percent on Monday morning.

The reversal came less than a week after the board had ruled out bringing Huang back. His ouster followed reports of an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Futurism says Nvidia's stock sank sharply, and because the chipmaker is so tied to the AI boom, the NASDAQ erased its gains for the year by Friday.

White House communications director Steven Cheung told Semafor that Trump was "totally involved" and that "we have to protect our geniuses." Trump told CNBC the board had asked for assurance on the national security threat, and that the administration provided it "with everything we know." He also said the company had "suffered greatly" over the two weeks.
Nvidia said in a press release that its investigation will continue and that Huang fully supports it and will cooperate. How much Trump's involvement shaped the board's decision remains unknown.

Democrats were furious. Senator Elizabeth Warren called the decision reckless and said Huang, executives and the board still owe Congress answers on export-control compliance. She also demanded that the administration explain what input senior officials gave. Representative Debbie Dingell said serious national security questions remain unanswered. Democrats have vowed to question Huang before Congress next year.

The episode lands amid a broader debate over chip sales to China. According to the New York Times, cited by Futurism, the Commerce Department approved the sale of nearly one million chips to Chinese companies earlier this year, then began closing regulatory loopholes last week.
de79ba5ddb88.summary: Nvidia's board reinstated CEO Jensen Huang after Trump joined a board meeting by phone, and shares surged over 34 percent. Democrats demand answers on national security and chip export controls.
de79ba5ddb88.pixel_take: Nothing says independent corporate governance like the president dialing into the board meeting. Somewhere, a stock chart is blushing and a compliance officer is quietly updating their résumé.
de79ba5ddb88.why_it_matters: Nvidia is so central to the AI trade that its leadership drama moved the whole NASDAQ, so anyone with index funds or a retirement account felt it. Government involvement in a company's boardroom raises questions about governance, export controls and political risk that investors now have to price in.
key_points: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang after Trump joined the meeting, and shares rose over 34 percent.
Nvidia's investigation continues, while Democrats like Warren and Dingell demand answers on national security and export controls.
The NASDAQ had wiped out its 2026 gains during the sell-off before the reversal.

6d192fa23bd1.headline: Bitcoin's Losing Streak Hits Second-Longest on Record, and Some Watchers Fear More Pain
body: Bitcoin is stuck in one of the longest losing runs in its history. According to CoinDesk's day-ahead briefing for Nov. 23, 2026, the current streak is the second-longest ever recorded, and some market observers see more downside ahead.

The source material is thin on specifics, so we can't say exactly how long the streak has lasted, how far prices have fallen or which analysts are sounding the alarm. What CoinDesk does make clear is the framing: this is a historically stubborn slide, and not everyone thinks the bottom is in.

Streaks like this matter because they test the patience of every type of holder. Long-term believers shrug and tell themselves it is just another chapter. Newer buyers, who may have arrived expecting a one-way escalator, tend to find out that bitcoin also has a basement, and that the elevator sometimes takes a while to come back.

As a general rule, extended losing runs can feed on themselves. Falling prices can trigger forced selling, dampen risk appetite and push traders to the sidelines, which can thin out buying interest. They can also set the stage for rebounds when sentiment gets bleak enough, though nothing in the material suggests when, or whether, that will happen here.

For now, the takeaway is caution. A record-adjacent streak is a notable data point, and the observers expecting further declines are a reminder that momentum, in either direction, rarely ends on a schedule.
6d192fa23bd1.summary: Bitcoin's current losing streak is the second-longest ever, according to CoinDesk, and some observers think prices could fall further. Details on the streak's size were not provided.
6d192fa23bd1.pixel_take: Bitcoin's losing streak is now a historical landmark. Unfortunately, it's the kind of landmark nobody wants to take a selfie in front of.
6d192fa23bd1.why_it_matters: Bitcoin's direction influences sentiment across the crypto market and the wallets of anyone holding digital assets. A historically long slide is a reminder that volatility cuts both ways, so position sizing and risk tolerance matter.
key_points: Bitcoin's losing streak is the second-longest ever, per CoinDesk.
Some market observers see further downside ahead.
The source gave no figures on the streak's length or price drop.

e8817cdb20a9.headline: Oath Keepers founder Stewart Rhodes says he's "absolutely done" with Trump
body: Stewart Rhodes, the founder of the right-wing extremist group the Oath Keepers, says he is no longer a supporter of President Donald Trump. According to The Hill, which cited an interview with The Associated Press, Rhodes said he is "absolutely done with" the president.

The material available is thin. The teaser does not say when the interview took place, what prompted the break, or what Rhodes plans to do next, so we will not guess at his reasons. The Hill describes the Oath Keepers as a right-wing extremist group.

Even so, the statement stands out because of who is making it. Rhodes has long been one of the better-known figures in the American far-right fringe, and public breaks between a president and parts of his most committed base tend to draw attention. They hint at how much cohesion exists in a political movement that often presents itself as unified.

Whether the split reflects wider frustration among Trump's most hardline backers or just one man's grievance cannot be told from this report. One interview is a data point, not a trend. Further reporting from the AP interview should clarify what Rhodes actually said and why.
e8817cdb20a9.summary: Oath Keepers founder Stewart Rhodes told The Associated Press he is "absolutely done with" President Trump, according to The Hill. The reasons were not given in the available material.
e8817cdb20a9.why_it_matters: Political rifts within a president's base can shape turnout, messaging and policy pressure, which in turn influence markets and regulatory expectations. One interview is no trend, but it is worth watching whether other hardline supporters voice similar doubts.
key_points: Stewart Rhodes, Oath Keepers founder, says he is "absolutely done with" Trump.
He made the remarks in an interview with The Associated Press, per The Hill.
The reasons for the break were not stated in the available material.

104765e3433c.headline: Amazon Reportedly Buying Decart's AI Chip Optimization Tech in Latest Talent Grab
body: Amazon is set to buy AI chip optimization technology from Decart, according to a report from Investing.com published on November 23, 2026. The outlet described the move as Amazon's latest grab for artificial intelligence talent.

The material available to us is thin. It does not include the price, the deal structure, the number of people involved, or a timeline for closing. We are not going to guess at any of that, and readers should treat the headline as the full extent of what has been confirmed.

What the headline does tell us is the target: technology that optimizes how AI workloads run on chips. In plain terms, this is software and know-how that squeezes more performance out of the same silicon. That matters because AI hardware is expensive and scarce, and efficiency gains can translate into real savings.

The 'talent grab' framing fits a wider pattern in tech. Big companies racing to build out their AI capabilities often buy small, specialized teams and their technology rather than build everything from scratch. It can be faster than hiring one engineer at a time, and it keeps rare expertise away from rivals.

For Amazon, better chip optimization could help it get more out of its AI infrastructure, though the source does not say how the technology will be used. Until Amazon or Decart supplies details, the key questions of price, scope and plans remain open.
104765e3433c.summary: Amazon is buying Decart's AI chip optimization technology, Investing.com reports, calling it the company's latest AI talent grab. Terms and plans were not disclosed in the available material.
104765e3433c.pixel_take: Amazon is shopping for people who can make chips work harder. Finally, someone in tech hunting for efficiency instead of just ordering more hardware.
104765e3433c.why_it_matters: AI hardware is costly and in demand, so software that extracts more performance from chips can lower costs and speed up products. Deals like this show how big tech competes for scarce AI expertise, which can shape which companies lead in AI infrastructure.
key_points: Amazon is to buy Decart's AI chip optimization technology, per Investing.com.
The deal is described as part of Amazon's ongoing AI talent grab.
Price, terms and integration plans were not provided in the material.

4df8b0a4ff06.headline: Jensen Huang's Nvidia Comeback Odds Reportedly Rise After Trump and Bessent Comments
body: The odds that Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang could return as the company's chief executive appeared to improve after fresh comments from President Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, according to The New York Times.

The headline alone raises an obvious puzzle: a return implies Huang is not currently in the job. The material available to us does not explain how or why he left the role, what the officials actually said, or when any comeback might happen, so we will not guess at those details.

What the report does establish is that two of the most senior figures in the U.S. government have weighed in on the question, and that the Times reads their remarks as a boost for a Huang return. When a president and a Treasury secretary comment on who runs a single company, it signals how much weight Washington places on the chip maker.

That attention fits a broader pattern. Nvidia sits at the center of the artificial intelligence boom, and its leadership is closely watched by investors, regulators and policymakers alike. Who holds the top job at such a company is not just a boardroom matter; it can shape market sentiment and the tone of the relationship with government.
For now, the story is a signal rather than a settled outcome. We will update as more details emerge on what was said and whether Nvidia itself responds.
4df8b0a4ff06.summary: The New York Times reports that comments by President Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent appeared to improve the chances of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang returning as chief executive.
4df8b0a4ff06.pixel_take: When the president and the Treasury secretary start weighing in on one company's corner office, you know it's not just any chip on the table.
4df8b0a4ff06.why_it_matters: Nvidia is a bellwether for the AI boom, so leadership questions can move investor sentiment and portfolios tied to tech. Government interest in its top job also shows how closely business and politics are now intertwined.
key_points: The New York Times says Huang's return odds appeared to rise.
The boost followed comments from President Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
Details of what was said and any timeline are not available.

0c1160d31848.headline: Moon Spuds Pass the Taste-Safety Test: Potatoes Grown in Fake Lunar Soil Are Safe to Eat
body: Potatoes grown in simulated moon soil are safe to eat, according to a new study from Oregon State University in the US, reported by Metro. The research, published in the journal npj Microgravity, suggests the humble spud could be a serious contender for future lunar menus.

The team, led by Professor Aymeric Goyer of the university's College of Agricultural Sciences and backed by Nasa funding, planted potatoes in lunar regolith simulants. Regolith is the loose rock and dust covering most of the moon's surface, and it contains very little organic matter. The researchers mixed in different levels of vermicompost, a nutrient-rich amendment made by using earthworms to break down organic material.

The amount mattered. Plants grown in simulants with 30% vermicompost matched the growth and development of those raised in Earth soil. Plants with no amendment were described as severely impaired, with stunting and underdeveloped roots, while those with 5% to 15% vermicompost recovered only partially.

Because moon dirt differs from place to place, the team tested five simulants representing both lunar mare and highland regions. They also grew potatoes in soil from Hermiston, Oregon, a region known for the highest potato yields in the world, as an Earth benchmark.

Safety was the other big question. Lunar regolith contains elevated levels of heavy metals, but the researchers believe organic matter helps by binding them, reducing damage to roots and growth. They found no statistically significant increase in glycoalkaloids, the natural potato toxins often linked to green discolouration under the skin.

The findings fit Nasa's Artemis goal of a sustained human presence on the moon, which would be far easier if food were produced there rather than shipped from Earth at great cost. The researchers say astronauts could carry a small amount of organic matter and then make more by converting food scraps and plant waste. Potatoes were chosen because they yield more calories per unit of land than many crops and are considered a practical staple for long missions.
0c1160d31848.summary: Oregon State University researchers found potatoes grown in simulated moon soil enriched with vermicompost matched Earth-grown plants and showed no significant rise in toxins, a step toward growing food for long lunar missions.
0c1160d31848.pixel_take: The Martian proved potatoes can survive on another world. Now science says the moon version won't poison you. Mash, boil, stick them in a lunar stew: the space race just got carb-loaded.
0c1160d31848.why_it_matters: Resupplying a lunar base from Earth is hugely expensive, so any way to grow food on site could cut mission costs. That matters for the commercial and government space sector, and for anyone watching the economics of long-term space exploration.
key_points: Potatoes in simulated lunar soil with 30% vermicompost grew as well as in Earth soil.
No statistically significant rise in glycoalkaloid toxins was found, despite heavy metals in regolith.
The work supports Nasa's Artemis aim of producing food on the moon instead of relying on resupply.

6c80453d9c99.headline: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX's AI arm over Grok's explicit deepfakes
body: The attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia have filed lawsuits against SpaceX Super Intelligence (SpaceXSI), Elon Musk's conglomerate company, according to Engadget. They accuse it of violating state consumer protection laws by letting users of its Grok AI chatbot create non-consensual sexually explicit content.

The suits allege the company released Grok's "spicy mode" to "push its lagging product to tens of millions of new users." They claim the feature enabled the creation of child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said in a press release that the case is about the millions of Virginians with accounts on X who were misled by false reassurances that their data and images would be safe. He said the company prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and deceived the public about it.

X Safety responded in a post that people using Grok for sexually explicit deepfakes "deliberately" violated the Terms of Service. It said it will keep testing and adjusting protections as abusers change tactics, and that CSAM has no place on X or in Grok. It also said it would take action, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement, when users get around safeguards.
The company has also gone on the offensive before: earlier this year SpaceXSI sued one of its own users for creating sexual images of real people without their consent.

Oregon and Virginia are not alone. The City of Baltimore has taken legal action, claiming Grok broke its Consumer Protection Ordinance, while the UK's media authority and the California attorney general have launched separate investigations into xAI and Grok.
6c80453d9c99.summary: Oregon and Virginia have sued SpaceX Super Intelligence, alleging Grok's explicit deepfake abilities violated consumer protection laws. The company says offenders broke its rules, and it faces other probes and suits.
6c80453d9c99.why_it_matters: Consumer protection suits from state attorneys general show that AI product design choices can carry real legal and financial risk. A growing pile of lawsuits and investigations could shape how AI companies build safeguards and how investors price regulatory exposure.
key_points: Oregon and Virginia sued SpaceXSI under state consumer protection laws over Grok's explicit content.
The suits say "spicy mode" was meant to grow users and enabled CSAM creation; X Safety says violators broke its terms.
Baltimore, UK's media authority and California's attorney general have also taken action or opened probes.

9c5f92f162b4.headline: Nvidia Jumps 35% on Jensen Huang's Return, Lifting Bitcoin While Anthropic Sits Out the Party
body: Nvidia shares surged 35% on news of Jensen Huang's return, according to Decrypt, sending chip stocks higher and giving Bitcoin a boost after a punishing selloff. Anthropic, which recently completed a record IPO, did not share in the gains and sank.

The material available is thin, so several details remain unclear, including what exactly Huang's return involves and over what period the 35% gain occurred. Decrypt's report frames the move as a comeback for Nvidia that spread across semiconductor stocks.

The Bitcoin angle is the more familiar part of the story. Crypto has often traded in step with tech and risk appetite, so when a heavyweight like Nvidia rallies, speculative assets tend to catch some of the lift. After a rough selloff, even a modest bounce reads as relief.

Anthropic's slide stands out because of the timing. A record IPO usually brings a wave of attention and enthusiasm, yet Decrypt says the company missed the rally. Newly listed stocks can be volatile, and the details behind the decline were not provided.

For now, the picture is of a market rewarding the chipmaker at the center of the AI hardware trade while a newly public AI company lags. Whether the rebound in Bitcoin lasts will likely depend on whether the tech momentum holds.
9c5f92f162b4.summary: Nvidia surged 35% on Jensen Huang's return, lifting chip stocks and Bitcoin after a selloff, Decrypt reports. Anthropic, fresh from a record IPO, sank and missed the rally.
9c5f92f162b4.pixel_take: Nvidia's boss comes back and the market throws a parade. Anthropic, freshly IPO'd, showed up to the party and apparently got stuck at the coat check.
9c5f92f162b4.why_it_matters: Nvidia's moves ripple across tech stocks and crypto, so a big swing can shift portfolios far beyond chip holders. The split between Nvidia and Anthropic is a reminder that AI enthusiasm is not lifting every boat equally.
key_points: Nvidia shares surged 35% on Jensen Huang's return, per Decrypt.
Bitcoin rose after a punishing selloff as chip stocks rallied.
Anthropic sank after its record IPO and missed the rally.

77ece0992320.headline: EU Unveils 22nd Sanctions Package, Vowing to Hit Russia's War Chest Harder
body: European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen has set out the EU's 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, according to The Guardian's live coverage of events in Europe. The stated aim is to keep up pressure on Moscow and strike harder at its ability to fund the war in Ukraine.

The material available does not spell out what the new package contains, so the specific measures, targets and timeline remain unclear. What is clear is the political message: Brussels wants to squeeze the revenue that pays for Russia's military campaign rather than simply add to the pile of existing restrictions.

Separately, Nato secretary general Mark Rutte stressed the need to secure the flow of crucial supplies to Ukraine, naming air defence weapons and ammunition. His remarks underline that the pressure on Russia is meant to run alongside practical military support for Kyiv.

Some context helps. EU sanctions packages generally need unanimous approval from member states, which often makes each round a negotiation. Reaching a 22nd package shows both the EU's persistence and the difficulty of finding fresh levers after so many rounds. Each new set tends to focus on closing loopholes and tightening areas where earlier measures leaked.
For now, this is an announcement of intent, not a finished deal. Whether the package is adopted as proposed, and how much it bites, will depend on talks among EU governments in the coming period.
77ece0992320.summary: Ursula von der Leyen presented the EU's 22nd sanctions package against Russia, aimed at hitting its ability to fund the Ukraine war, while Nato's Mark Rutte urged steady supplies of air defence and ammunition to Ukraine.
77ece0992320.why_it_matters: Sanctions on Russia influence energy, trade and financial markets across Europe, and each new package can shift risk for companies with exposure to the region. Continued pressure and military aid also signal that the war's costs for governments and taxpayers are far from over.
key_points: Von der Leyen presented the EU's 22nd sanctions package against Russia.
The goal is to strike harder at Russia's ability to fund the war in Ukraine.
Nato's Rutte stressed securing air defence weapons and ammunition for Ukraine.

aa93777566bc.headline: Trump backs Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO, says US has no evidence of wrongdoing
body: President Donald Trump on Monday publicly endorsed Nvidia's decision to reinstate founder Jensen Huang as CEO and president, writing on Truth Social that the US government has no reason to believe his return poses any national security risk, according to TechCrunch.

Nvidia's board had said its own decision followed consultations with senior levels of the US government, which concluded the reinstatement was not a security risk. Trump went further, claiming Attorney General Todd Blanche had confirmed the government has no evidence Huang engaged in unlawful conduct. TechCrunch notes that is unusual, since the attorney general typically runs such investigations independently, and Blanche has not yet made a formal statement.
Trump may have seen it coming. Over the weekend he told a PBS journalist that Huang was "back where he should be," and when asked whether that meant a reinstatement, he replied "I hope so."

The backdrop is messy. Huang was accused of multiple extramarital relationships, including with a direct report and another employee. The most worrying was a relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company that bought billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips and who has been described as an alleged Chinese spy. That raised questions over whether sensitive information or China's access to export-restricted AI chips could be at risk.

Trump said last week that nobody had proven she is a spy, adding that China and the US both "play games" with each other. In his statement he called Huang a "Great Patriot and National Treasure," yet urged Nvidia to continue its internal investigation into its compliance with US export controls.
aa93777566bc.summary: Trump praised Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO, saying the government has no evidence of wrongdoing, while urging the company to continue its export-control compliance probe. The attorney general hasn't yet commented formally.
aa93777566bc.pixel_take: Nvidia's board consulted the government, the president pre-announced the verdict on PBS, and the attorney general is still reading his mail. Corporate governance, now with a Truth Social press office.
aa93777566bc.why_it_matters: Nvidia is central to the AI chip boom, so leadership turmoil and export-control questions can move markets and supply chains. Presidential involvement in what is normally an independent legal process adds political uncertainty for investors watching chip policy toward China.
key_points: Trump endorsed Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO and president, citing no national security risk.
He said the attorney general found no evidence of unlawful conduct, though Blanche hasn't formally commented.
Trump urged Nvidia to continue its internal export-control compliance investigation.

fa69809e3f31.headline: Nikki Haley Says Trump Handed Putin a 'Winner' Look at Summit
body: Former U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley said on Sunday that President Donald Trump made Russian President Vladimir Putin look like a "winner" during trilateral talks earlier this month, according to The Hill.

The teaser describes the talks as involving Chinese officials, and Haley's comments appear to center on the relationship between China and Russia. The text of her remarks was cut off in the material available, so the full reasoning behind her criticism is not clear here.
